title: Algorithmic Accountability Without Bureaucratic Paralysis: Governance Frameworks for Mid-Market Enterprises

detail.title: Algorithmic Accountability Without Bureaucratic Paralysis: Governance Frameworks for Mid-Market Enterprises
detail.abstract: The proliferation of AI governance frameworks over the past five years has produced a robust toolkit for responsible AI deployment-but one designed almost exclusively for organizations with the resources to use it. Frameworks from NIST, the EU AI Act's compliance requirements, and corporate responsible AI programs from Google, Microsoft, and Meta presuppose dedicated ethics teams, specialized legal counsel, compliance infrastructure, and organizational bandwidth that mid-market enterprises (500-5,000 employees) simply do not possess. Yet mid-market enterprises face the same legal, reputational, and operational risks from AI deployment as their larger counterparts-and are increasingly deploying AI systems in customer-facing, employment-affecting, and operationally consequential contexts. This paper addresses the mid-market AI governance gap by proposing the Lightweight AI Governance Framework (LAGF), a three-mechanism governance system designed for organizations that cannot afford enterprise-grade AI governance but cannot afford to operate without governance. The three mechanisms are: (1) Decision-Context Classification-a triage system that routes AI decisions to appropriate oversight levels based on consequence severity, eliminating the need for uniform governance intensity across all AI applications; (2) Embedded Accountability-integrating governance checkpoints into existing product development and procurement workflows rather than creating parallel governance structures; and (3) Incident Learning Loopslightweight post-incident review processes modeled on aviation safety practices that build organizational learning from AI failures without requiring dedicated governance personnel. The framework is illustrated through implementation cases in mid-market financial services, logistics, and healthcare companies. The paper concludes with implications for CEOs and CTOs designing governance for resource-constrained organizations, compliance officers adapting enterprise frameworks for mid-market realities, and management consultants advising mid-market clients on AI governance.

title:
Ephemeral Agent Credentialing: A Security Architecture Pattern for Autonomous AI Agents 
With a Case Study of CVE-2025-68664 (LangGrinch) and a Reference Implementation in Go

detail.title:
Ephemeral Agent Credentialing: A Security Architecture Pattern for Autonomous AI Agents 
With a Case Study of CVE-2025-68664 (LangGrinch) and a Reference Implementation in Go

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No external funding. Independent research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a security architecture pattern paper with a software case study; no human subjects, clinical data, or animal research is involved.
declarations.funderStatement: No funder. Independent research.

detail.abstract:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly perform privileged operations on sensitive systems, yet most production deployments still authenticate them with long-lived API keys, shared service accounts, or OAuth access tokens whose lifetimes vastly exceed the agents' own. When an agent task completes in two minutes but its credentials remain valid for fifteen, the resulting "credential exposure window" is an attack surface that scales with agent concurrency. Recent incidents such as CVE-2025-68664 ("LangGrinch"), a serialization flaw in langchain-core that enabled environment-variable exfiltration via prompt-steered deserialization, illustrate how rapidly this surface converts into full cloud-credential disclosure.

This paper introduces Ephemeral Agent Credentialing, a security architecture pattern that eliminates long-lived agent secrets by binding credentials to individual agent tasks rather than agent identities or deployment roles. The pattern is composed of eight coordinated components: ephemeral identity issuance via platform attestation, short-lived task-scoped JWTs, zero-trust validation with mTLS, multi-level revocation, tamper-evident audit logging, agent-to-agent mutual authentication, cryptographic delegation-chain verification, and operational observability built on RFC 7807 error contracts. We formalise a threat model covering external credential theft, compromised agent instances, lateral movement, insider abuse, and cross-agent privilege escalation, and identify the threats explicitly out of scope. We then present AgentWrit, a source-available reference implementation in Go (PolyForm Internal Use 1.0.0) that realises the pattern as a single-binary broker with SPIFFE-based identity, EdDSA-signed JWTs, four-level revocation, scope-attenuated delegation, and hash-chained audit logs. A post-hoc analysis of CVE-2025-68664 quantifies how each of the eight components reduces or eliminates the incident's blast radius. The paper contributes an implementation-level specification that maps directly to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026), NIST IR 8596, and the IETF WIMSE architecture, alongside a workflow-level migration playbook framed around the position that ephemeral credentialing is a design choice made at first agent deployment rather than a phased remediation roadmap.

title: AI-Driven Transaction Monitoring Systems (AI-TMS): Reducing False Positives and Enhancing Financial Crime Detection Through Data Integration and Machine Learning

detail.title: AI-Driven Transaction Monitoring Systems (AI-TMS): Reducing False Positives and Enhancing Financial Crime Detection Through Data Integration and Machine Learning
detail.abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) transaction monitoring systems at most U.S. financial institutions remain dominated by static, threshold-based rule logic. The operational consequence is well documented: industry false-positive rates routinely exceed ninety percent, investigator capacity is consumed by alert disposition rather than financial-crime intelligence, and downstream Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) are degraded in quality before they ever reach the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). This paper proposes an AI-Driven Transaction Monitoring System (AI-TMS) ─ a hybrid architecture that combines integrated data engineering, supervised and unsupervised machine learning, network analytics, and explainability controls that materially reduce false positives without sacrificing recall, regulatory transparency, or audit defensibility. Through a reproducible simulation grounded in canonical AML typologies (structuring, mule activity, velocity spikes, cross-border layering), the framework demonstrates 30-40 percent reductions in false positives and 20-30 percent improvements in detection precision, with corresponding gains in investigator output. The framework aligns with the AML Act of 2020, FinCEN's 2021 National AML/CFT Priorities, and FinCEN's 2024 proposed rule modernizing AML/CFT program requirements. The contribution is a practitioner-oriented architecture and evaluation protocol that institutions can deploy within existing regulatory frameworks.

title: Territorial Algorithmic Invisibility: A Diagnostic Framework for Generative Engine Optimization Applied to Local Tourism Destination Entities
affiliations: Criamente Digital Brand Architecture

detail.title: Territorial Algorithmic Invisibility: A Diagnostic Framework for Generative Engine Optimization Applied to Local Tourism Destination Entities
detail.abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) as primary mediators of travel information retrieval presents a distinct challenge for local tourism destinations: algorithmic invisibility induced not by poor content production, but by geographic proximity to dominant destinations that systematically absorb a smaller entity's algorithmic identity. This paper introduces the concept of Territorial Algorithmic Invisibility (TAI) and proposes the Destination Algorithmic Readiness Score (DARS), a five-dimensional diagnostic framework for measuring and addressing GEO deficiencies in Destination Marketing Organizations (DMOs). The framework is derived from a structured diagnostic audit of Neltur, the official tourism company of Niterói, Rio de Janeiro-a destination of demonstrable cultural and geographic significance that exists in the algorithmic shadow of its neighboring metropolis. Systematic querying of ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Perplexity AI revealed that Niterói attractions are consistently attributed to Rio de Janeiro or omitted entirely from AI-generated travel recommendations, despite housing internationally recognized architectural landmarks including Oscar Niemeyer's Museu de Arte Contemporânea (MAC). The DARS baseline established for Niterói (38/100) quantifies the gap between the destination's real-world tourism value and its current algorithmic representation. The paper contributes to the nascent GEO literature by extending existing frameworks beyond brand and professional entities to geographic destinations, formalizing the Proximity Shadow Effect as a structural impediment to local DMO visibility, and proposing a reproducible diagnostic methodology applicable to tourism entities globally.

title: Testing the Aesthetic-to-Risk Framework: A Protocol for Qualitative Multimedia Content Analysis of Nihilistic Violence Aesthetics in Public Reddit Posts

detail.title: Testing the Aesthetic-to-Risk Framework: A Protocol for Qualitative Multimedia Content Analysis of Nihilistic Violence Aesthetics in Public Reddit Posts
detail.abstract: This protocol describes a planned empirical study designed to apply and test the Aesthetic-to-Risk Framework of Nihilistic Violence Aesthetics (ART-NVA) through qualitative multimedia content analysis of public Reddit posts. ART-NVA was developed as a conceptual framework for interpreting how nihilistic violent meaning may be communicated through meaning collapse, anti-human or dehumanizing orientation, aesthetic packaging of violence, irony and ambiguity as communicative shields, and proximity to warning-behavior signaling. Existing scholarship has examined extremist memes, hybridized extremism, toxic multimodal content, online radicalization, and threat-assessment warning behaviors, but these literatures have not yet been fully integrated into a framework for studying nihilistic violence aesthetics as a distinct public online communication pattern. The proposed study will examine a purposive sample of public Reddit submissions collected during a fixed sampling window and coded using the ART-NVA codebook. The unit of analysis will be one public Reddit submission, including title, body text, embedded media, meme text, and visible post-level cues. Analysis will use manifest qualitative coding, descriptive counts, co-occurrence review, evidence anchors, and typology development. The study does not seek to identify extremists, classify groups, predict violence, or assess individual risk. Instead, it is designed to evaluate whether ART-NVA can be applied systematically to public online content and to support future empirical refinement of the framework.

title: Knowledge without Borders: The Role of Academia in Shaping a Resilient Global Future
affiliations: and Tilak Maharashtra Vidyapeeth

detail.title: Knowledge without Borders: The Role of Academia in Shaping a Resilient Global Future
detail.abstract: In today’s interconnected world, resilience is not a localized concept but a global imperative. As societies navigate an increasingly complex and fragile ecosystem shaped by rapid climate shifts, geopolitical uncertainties, public health crises, and technological disruptions, the role of academia in shaping global resilience is more crucial than ever. This paper explores how academic institutions—universities, research centers, and think tanks—have become pivotal in preparing humanity for resilient futures through the transnational production, dissemination, and democratization of knowledge. Through a qualitative approach that incorporates policy document analysis, international case studies, and literature synthesis, the study introduces the Abstract Academic Resilience Partnership Model (ARPM), providing a comprehensive framework for understanding how academic ecosystems contribute to adaptive capacity building, inclusive education, open knowledge systems, and sustainable development. The paper emphasizes the urgency of integrating academia more deeply into global resilience planning through supportive policy frameworks, especially in underrepresented regions. It concludes with strategic recommendations for strengthening academic diplomacy and enhancing the role of global education networks in constructing a shared, secure, and resilient future.

title: Trustworthy Transaction Arena (TTA): A Governance Architecture for Multi-Actor Agentic AI Systems with Probabilistic Workflow Verification

detail.title: Trustworthy Transaction Arena (TTA): A Governance Architecture for Multi-Actor Agentic AI Systems with Probabilistic Workflow Verification

detail.abstract: Existing multi-agent frameworks evaluate correctness only at the team outcome level: if the agent team achieves its goal, the transaction is deemed successful. This is insufficient for business and social activities, which consist of multiple interrelated tasks — involving asynchronous, time-constrained, and probabilistic behaviors — pursued toward broader goals. Without a framework that conveys objectives and authority to every actor throughout the activity, the means by which goals are achieved cannot be verified. This paper proposes the Trustworthy Transaction Arena (TTA), treating these activities as governed workflows in which every actor operates under delegated authority from a human principal, subject to continuous enforcement at every step. Its principal features — absent from all existing approaches — are: (i) a Unified Governance Layer combining static role-based and dynamic workflow-state access control in a single enforcement layer through which every actor action must pass; (ii) Non-Escalation of Delegated Authority (NEDA) — no agent can exceed the authority scope of its delegating principal — enforced transitively throughout the entire delegation chain; and (iii) a HERT probabilistic workflow engine handling asynchronous and stochastic behaviors, enabling critical path identification, bottleneck extraction, and detection of stochastic behaviors such as hallucination and capability leakage, with structural human supervision checkpoints. The architecture extends two production-validated prior works — the CBA access control model extended to cascaded AI agent delegation [Kitajima2002], and the HERT probabilistic formalism extended to stochastic workflow verification in AI environments [Kitajima1981-HERT] — and is demonstrated through an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest emergency response application.

detail.title: Economics of Smart Products with Machine Learning Forthcoming in Production Operations and Management

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Production and Operations Management

detail.abstract: Driven by advances in machine learning (ML), smart products improve over time through data-driven insights as ongoing user interactions generate usage data that enable the training, evaluation, and refinement of underlying algorithms. However, when firms implement strategies to collect more data to enhance product quality and profits, they must also consider strategic consumer behavior that may lead to unintended negative consequences. Specifically, consumers may intentionally postpone purchases in the early stages of a product's development, anticipating future quality improvements and price reductions, which in turn complicates data collection during this critical period. Considering advancements in disruptive technologies, this study examines the critical yet underexplored economic impact of ML on pricing strategies. Few studies have focused on how ML influences profit maximization in the presence of strategic consumers. To address this gap, we develop two-period game-theoretic models that employ two dynamic pricing strategies, responsive versus preannounced pricing, to investigate how firms developing smart products adapt to the disruptive impact of ML, considering the behavior of strategic consumers. Our study provides several significant implications. First, we find that ML impacts firms' profits by impacting consumers' strategic behaviors in opposite directions. Second, under both dynamic pricing strategies, prices may initially be low and may either rise or decline over time. Third, we demonstrate that, different from findings in the existing literature on strategic consumer behavior, preannounced pricing policies are generally not optimal for the firm when its ability to leverage ML is relatively limited, and consumers are less strategic. Overall, this study makes three contributions to the literature. First, we clarify the impact of ML on a smart product firm's profit. We find two effects in the application of ML: 1) a positive effect associated with ML (the "ML + effect") and 2) a negative effect (the "ML-effect"). Second, this study highlights a fundamental economic mechanism for smart products in the presence of strategic consumers. Finally, it provides a decision-making tool for smart product firms to select an optimal dynamic pricing strategy.

detail.abstract: The worldwide push for sustainability and climate-smart investments has sparked a real demand for financial systems we can trust and see through clearly. Enter blockchain-powered green bonds: a fresh way to make eco-friendly funding smoother and more believable. This paper examines how blockchain and digital tools are energizing the green bond space through transparent visibility, easy tracking, robust reporting and true accountability. It also looks at how smart contracts and distributed ledger tech (DLT) streamline operations and sharpen oversight in the sustainable finance world. Drawing from secondary sources like reports from institutions, research on green finance, blockchain papers, and green bond analyses, the work gauges blockchain's impact on boosting investor faith, market speed, live tracking, and curbing greenwashing. We apply comparative and stats-based methods to spot shifts since blockchain joined the green bond party. Results reveal that these blockchain-driven platforms ramp up transparency with tamper-proof, instant logs of money flows and eco-metrics. Smart contracts speed up reports and handle compliance on autopilot, while DLT nails fund paths and check-ins. And, by making ESG information more authentic and reliable, blockchain verifications reduce the risks of greenwashing. Better access to true sustainability details builds investor confidence and draws more folks into green projects. For regulators, banks, policymakers, and eco-investors aiming to toughen green finance rules, this offers key takeaways. Blockchain setups promise clearer reports, sharper monitoring, and faster growth for sustainable investing. In the end, blending blockchain with green bonds marks a big leap to safer, more responsible, tech-fueled finance.

title: Explainability, Transparency, and Accountability in AI Systems

detail.title: Explainability, Transparency, and Accountability in AI Systems

detail.abstract:
Background. Explainability, transparency, and accountability have evolved from research aspirations to binding regulatory requirements for AI systems deployed in high-stakes domains. Article 86 of the EU AI Act, clarified by the political agreement on the Digital Omnibus reached on 7 May 2026, establishes a binding right for affected individuals to an explanation in high-risk AI decisions. The Court of Justice of the European Union's judgment in Case C-203/22 has confirmed the right to explanation under Article 15(1)(h) of the General Data Protection Regulation. The technical landscape of explainable AI, anchored by methods including LIME, SHAP, and the DARPA Explainable AI programme, has matured substantially but continues to face structural challenges in producing explanations that are simultaneously faithful, comprehensible, and actionable.

Purpose. This paper synthesises the explainability, transparency, and accountability literature applicable to deployed AI systems, examining post-hoc and intrinsic explainability methods, adversarial attacks on explanation and fairness mechanisms, regulatory transparency requirements and their operational feasibility, accountability architectures including audit trails and human oversight, and the specific challenges of explaining agentic AI behaviour as distinct from single-prediction explanation.

Approach. The paper adopts a narrative literature review methodology drawing on authoritative primary sources, including foundational explainable AI research (Ribeiro, Singh, & Guestrin, 2016; Lundberg & Lee, 2017; Gunning et al., 2019), recent agentic explainability research, the EU AI Act with the May 2026 Digital Omnibus implementation timeline, the EDPB Opinion 28/2024, the CJEU judgment in Case C-203/22, and operational guidance from ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.

Findings. Three findings are advanced. First, post-hoc explainability methods, including LIME and SHAP, are operationally available but do not guarantee the faithfulness, stability, or comprehensibility of their explanations, and are themselves subject to adversarial manipulation. Second, regulatory transparency obligations under the EU AI Act Article 86, the GDPR, and equivalent frameworks impose operational requirements that current explainable AI technology cannot fully satisfy, creating an implementation gap that organisations must bridge through governance practice. Third, explaining agentic AI behaviour requires explaining sequences of actions and their justifications, rather than single predictions, a frontier for which current explanation methods are inadequate.

Implications. Practitioners deploying high-risk AI systems require integrated explainability architectures that combine technical XAI methods, audit logging sufficient to support post-hoc investigation, human oversight that meets the meaningfulness requirements of Article 14 of the EU AI Act, and continuous monitoring designed to detect explanation degradation and adversarial manipulation. The paper proposes an explainability control architecture mapping technical, governance, and regulatory dimensions for practitioner use.

title:
Access to Justice in the Age of AI:
Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and University of Southern California

detail.title:
Access to Justice in the Age of AI:
Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts
detail.abstract: This paper studies how generative AI has reshaped entry into the federal civil court system. Drawing on administrative records covering more than 4.5 million non-prisoner federal civil court cases from FY2005-FY2026 and 46 million PACER docket entries matched to those cases, we document three sets of findings. First, the number of pro se cases-or self-represented cases-is increasing dramatically, rising from a long-term steady-state average of 11% to 16.8% in FY2025. This increase is concentrated in case types characterized by formulaic document production and absent from more complex, attorney-intensive categories. Second, we argue these cases are placing a larger burden on federal district courts. Pro se cases are not terminating faster, and this combined with the increased case numbers suggests more cases for judges to process. Moreover, intra-case activity is up, with the total volume of docket entries per court generated by pro se cases in their first 180 days up 158% from pre-AI means to 2025. Third, we directly validate that AI use is increasing in federal courts. Using a random sample of 1,600 complaints drawn from an 8-year period (2019-2026), we find that a large and growing share of complaints are flagging positive for AI-generated text, from essentially zero in the pre-AI period to more than 18% in 2026.

title: The Human Data Collective v2: A Revised Architecture for Contributor-Owned Machine Intelligence With Provider Independent Data, Compute, and Feedback Layers for Public Good AI

detail.title: The Human Data Collective v2: A Revised Architecture for Contributor-Owned Machine Intelligence With Provider Independent Data, Compute, and Feedback Layers for Public Good AI
detail.abstract: Several of the biggest challenges plaguing the development and utilization of language models in 2026, notably bias, the difficulty of monitoring undesirable and illegal content, psychological safety risks associated with human led alignment, and severe environmental impact, can be partially or completely mitigated through the careful curation of high quality human generated data, more efficient models, and fair incentives. This second version of the Human Data Collective builds on the first by removing any dependency on centralized frontier providers and adding a contribution layer of connected inference nodes. It proposes an approach to incentives that compensates contributors for their work through the Human Data Collective Token, and shifts to the use of smaller, more efficient language models, trained on category-specific datasets.

title: Operationalising Pillar 6 of Ghana's National AI Strategy in Insurance A Trust-first Blueprint for Sector Adoption
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Operationalising Pillar 6 of Ghana's National AI Strategy in Insurance A Trust-first Blueprint for Sector Adoption
detail.abstract: Ghana's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035, released by the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations on 12 December 2025 and publicly launched in Accra on 24 April 2026, commits the country to building AI that understands local languages, reflects local culture and is trained on Ghanaian data (Government of Ghana, 2025). Pillar 6 of the Strategy targets sector adoption, identifying insurance among its priority domains. This paper translates that ambition into an operational blueprint for the insurance sector. The argument is empirical, regulatory, theoretical and practical. Empirically, doctoral research on digital insurance adoption in Ghana finds that, when tested simultaneously, consumer trust is a stronger predictor of adoption attitudes than perceived usefulness, that ease of use is non-significant, and that infrastructure exerts a direct effect on adoption independent of attitudes and intentions (Botchey, 2025a). Theoretically, the paper extends the vendor trust compensatory regime (Botchey, 2025b) to AI-mediated insurance interactions, drawing on the established literatures on institutional voids (Khanna & Palepu, 1997, 2010), trust-integrated technology acceptance (Gefen, Karahanna, & Straub, 2003; Pavlou, 2003) and the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (Venkatesh, Morris, Davis, & Davis, 2003), and reframes AI adoption in Ghanaian insurance as a trustengineering problem rather than a capabilities problem. Regulatorily, the existing supervisory framework under the Insurance Act, 2021 (Act 1061) and the National Insurance Commission is shown to be a sufficient platform for AI integration, provided that sector-specific guidance is issued in parallel with the forthcoming Emerging Technologies Bill and informed by international precedents including the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority's opinion on AI governance (EIOPA, 2025) and the Financial Stability Institute's comparative review of AI in finance (FSI, 2024). Practically, the paper proposes a five-layer blueprint covering language and data, products, governance, skills and measurement. It also identifies a structural gap between the Strategy's ambition and the demonstrated readiness of public-facing AI systems, drawing on the publicly discussed launch of the Aku assistant to argue that local private-sector actors have a comparative advantage in implementation. The contribution is a regulator-implementable roadmap that aligns the Strategy's national objectives with the operational realities of an industry whose gross-premium penetration was 1.0 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 0.63 per cent on an IFRS 17 Insurance Service Revenue basis, highlighting that AI-enabled distribution must address structural under-penetration rather than only efficiency at current scale. Although the empirical setting is Ghana, the blueprint and the underlying regime classification are intended to be portable: the analytical pattern of Regime B and Regime C is encountered in many emerging-market insurance jurisdictions, and the paper aims to offer a transferable template for regulators in comparable institutional settings. The paper concludes with policy recommendations addressed to the National Insurance Commission, the Responsible AI Authority, insurers and brokers, and the Actuarial Society of Ghana.

detail.abstract:
The audit and assurance profession is undergoing a long-arc transition from periodic event-bound assurance toward continuous monitoring with always-on verification. This transition has been advocated in the continuous-audit literature for over two decades but has been technologically constrained by the limitations of rule-based monitoring tools. We argue in this paper that the recent maturation of survival analysis methodology, federated learning, and privacy-preserving aggregation primitives is sufficient to remove this technological constraint and to enable a substantive shift to predictive compliance: a regime in which compliance state degradation is forecast statistically and surfaced to verifiers ahead of conventional re-verification cycles. 

We develop the case for predictive compliance from the audit and assurance perspective. We frame compliance state degradation as a time-to-event problem amenable to survival analysis. We discuss how the calibrated-threshold mechanism of predictive alerting can be tied to audit-team operational capacity. We analyse the implications of federated cross-organisation pattern inference for cross-firm assurance and for jurisdictional cooperation. We address the practitioner concerns most likely to arise in adoption: liability allocation when predictions are wrong; auditor judgment in the face of statistical alerts; the relationship between predictive alerting and the established audit standards (ISA, GAAS, ISAE); and the supervisory expectations under which firms will be held responsible for compliance failures that predictive alerting did or did not surface. 

We make three policy recommendations: (i) audit and accounting standard-setters should issue guidance on predictive compliance practices including the use of statistical alert systems alongside conventional reverification; (ii) regulators should clarify supervisory expectations on the use of predictive alerts and on liability allocation when alerts are or are not generated; (iii) audit firms should invest in cross-firm benchmarking of predictive alerting outcomes to support quality standardisation across the profession. 

The paper contributes to the continuous-audit research agenda by providing a unified statistical framing for predictive compliance and by addressing the policy and professional-practice implications. It complements the technical and economic threads of work developed in companion papers in this series.

title: Privacy-Preserving Compliance: A Cryptographic Framework for Selective Disclosure in Regulated Markets

detail.title: Privacy-Preserving Compliance: A Cryptographic Framework for Selective Disclosure in Regulated Markets

detail.abstract:
Compliance verification in regulated markets requires that verifiers obtain confidence in an entity's regulatory status before making downstream decisions. The conventional resolution of this requirement is full disclosure of underlying evidence to each verifier on each verification occasion, with substantial cost to the entity's informational privacy and substantial duplication of sensitive-data storage across verifier organisations. Modern cryptography offers, in principle, the tools to better balance verifier information needs against entity privacy: zero-knowledge proof systems, selective-disclosure credentials, vector commitments, and privacy-preserving aggregation primitives are now mature enough for serious regulatory consideration. Yet the legal and regulatory frameworks under which these tools would be deployed have not caught up with their technical readiness.
We develop the legal and policy case for adoption of a cryptographic framework for selective disclosure in regulated markets. We analyse the framework's interaction with data-protection law (UK GDPR, EU GDPR, US state-level privacy regimes), financial-services regulation (FATF Recommendations, FCA rules, BSA/AML obligations), employment law (right-to-work, employment background screening), and identity system regulation (eIDAS 2.0, US REAL ID, digital identity wallets). We identify the principal legal uncertainties that constrain adoption and propose specific reforms to resolve them: data-protection safe harbours for cryptographic verification protocols; reconceiving regulatory data-retention requirements in terms of cryptographic attestations rather than underlying evidence; standardising regulator-grade revocation mechanisms; clarifying the legal status of zero-knowledge proofs as admissible evidence in supervisory and enforcement actions.
We make four policy recommendations: (i) data-protection regulators (ICO, EDPB, equivalent) should issue guidance affirming that cryptographic selective-disclosure protocols meeting specified properties are compliant with data-protection law; (ii) financial-services regulators should issue guidance clarifying that cryptographic attestations satisfying specified properties can substitute for evidence retention obligations under AML/KYC rules; (iii) standard-setters should coordinate cross-jurisdictional protocol standards through W3C, IETF, and ISO/TC 307 with regulator participation; (iv) legislators in jurisdictions with active digital-identity programmes (UK, EU, US, Singapore) should ensure that statutory frameworks accommodate selective-disclosure verification.
The paper contributes to the law-and-economics literature on data sharing under privacy constraints, to the policy economics of RegTech, and to the legal-academic literature on emerging-technology regulation. It complements the technical and economic threads of work developed in companion papers in this series.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a routine source of health information, reassurance, triage support, and clinical decision support. Health communication scholarship has begun to examine AI as a source of information and trust, but current adoption debates remain too concentrated on accuracy, explainability, and user acceptance. This theoretical and applied article argues that AI-mediated health communication also requires an identity-based adoption lens. Trust determines whether patients, caregivers, and clinicians are willing to consider AI guidance; identity helps determine whether the communicated guidance becomes self-relevant, repeatable, and behaviorally durable. Drawing on health communication theory, identity-based motivation, self-determination theory, human-automation trust, and digital behavior-change scholarship, the article proposes the Identity Activation Loop as a communication-centered operating model. The model describes six stages through which AI-mediated health messages may support durable but governed behavior: stimulus, identity cue, social or clinical feedback, internalization, repeated safe behavior, and identity stabilization. The article develops propositions and measurement implications for studying AI-mediated health communication, including trust calibration, limit awareness, appropriate escalation to human care, reduced prompt dependence, and private follow-through. The central claim is that health AI should not be evaluated only by whether users engage with a system, but by whether communication produces safe, identity-consistent, and clinically accountable behavior.

detail.abstract:
Objective: To estimate, using a decision-analytic model, which hypothetical payer acquisition costs for enobosarm (a non-FDA-approved SARM) would produce acceptable incremental cost-effectiveness versus resistance exercise training (RET) and versus no treatment for sarcopenia in community-dwelling US adults aged ≥65 years, treating drug price as a threshold parameter rather than an empirical input. 

Background: Sarcopenia carries substantial morbidity and cost. Resistance exercise training (RET) has trial support; enobosarm lacks FDA approval for sarcopenia, so no legitimate market acquisition price exists. Comparisons therefore reduce to threshold-style questions: conditional on hypothetical payer prices and RET delivery costs, when does incremental cost-effectiveness favor one strategy? 

Methods: Three-arm decision-tree model (US payer; 3-year horizon) comparing enobosarm, RET, and a no-treatment natural history reference. Costs and QALYs discounted at 3%/year (US Second Panel reference case). Primary policy output: mapping of hypothetical annual enobosarm acquisition cost to ICERs and dominance (Figure 1). Sequential ICER analysis identifies dominated strategies. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA; 10,000 draws, all parameters varied) produces cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) for all three comparisons. Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) estimated per patient. Budget impact analysis across 0-100% adoption rates in a hypothetical 10,000-patient health system. Python code provided for replication. 

Results: Three-arm sequential ICER analysis: RET is simply dominated by enobosarm at the US$720/year illustrative acquisition anchor (enobosarm cheaper at US$2,196 vs US$2,355 and higher QALYs at 2.171 vs 2.136 over 3 discounted years). Enobosarm ICER versus no-treatment: US$45,923/QALY (DC +US$2,196; DE +0.048 QALYs). Threshold sweep: enobosarm dominance over RET fails above approximately US$780/year annual acquisition at these effectiveness inputs. PSA: enobosarm cost-effective versus RET in 73.6% of draws at US$100,000/QALY; versus no-treatment in 56.0% of draws. EVPI: US$6,748/patient at US$100,000/QALY, indicating substantial residual decision uncertainty. Budget impact at 100% adoption: -US$560,000/year system-wide savings versus RET in a 10,000-patient cohort (all adoption rates cost-saving).

Conclusions: Reframed as threshold analysis, the study estimates which hypothetical acquisition costs change incremental conclusions versus RET and versus no treatment. Enobosarm at US$45,923/QALY versus no treatment — at the illustrative US$720/year acquisition anchor — approaches common willingness-to-pay thresholds; whether this is achievable depends on future regulatory approval and pricing. High EVPI signals that better data on effectiveness and utility transitions would materially change the decision.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether geopolitical commodity shocks produce scale-dependent dependence between energy and technology markets, and whether the recovered dependence has meaningful implications for financial tail risk. Using high-dimensional daily panels spanning 2020 to 2026, we combine local projections, generalized Morse wavelets, and scale-specific canonical correlation analysis under classical, ridge, and sparse regularization. We find that short-horizon dependence is dense, while the quarterly band becomes sparse and low-rank. The recovered long-horizon direction survives randomization-based inference and translates into economically meaningful downside risk for semiconductor-sector exposures under severe geopolitical stress.

title: Export Instability, Market Concentration and Resilience in Indian Small Cardamom Trade under Global Shocks

detail.title: Export Instability, Market Concentration and Resilience in Indian Small Cardamom Trade under Global Shocks
detail.abstract: Global shocks increasingly influence the performance and stability of export-oriented agricultural commodities through disruptions in trade logistics, market access, transportation systems and international demand conditions. Indian small cardamom exports experienced substantial structural changes during the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent geopolitical disturbances, particularly the Russia-Ukraine war and conflicts in West Asia. Against this background, the present study examined the growth, instability, resilience, market concentration and trade direction of Indian small cardamom exports during 2010-11 to 2024-25 by classifying the study period into a Stable Regime (2010-11 to 2018-19) and a Shock & Adjustment Regime (2019-20 to 2024-25). Secondary data on export quantity, export value and unit value were collected from official trade databases and analyzed using compound annual growth rate, Cuddy-Della Valle instability index, Coppock instability index, Export Resilience Index (ERI), Hazell decomposition analysis, Hirschman concentration index and Markov chain analysis.

title: The Price of Fiscal Confusion: Evidence from U.S. Treasury Communication
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University and

detail.title: The Price of Fiscal Confusion: Evidence from U.S. Treasury Communication
detail.abstract: While the macroeconomic transmission of central bank forward guidance is well documented, the operational footprint of sovereign fiscal communication remains largely a black box. Does the macroeconomic penalty for erratic fiscal signaling change when the fundamental institutional anchor shifts? We answer this by applying large language models (LLMs) to 11,691 U.S. Department of the Treasury press releases from 1996 to 2026, extracting a high-frequency, multidimensional history of U.S. fiscal posture. Utilizing a state-dependent local projections (SDLP) framework, augmented by novel historical decompositions, we identify a clear structural break in how the macroeconomy absorbs fiscal uncertainty. We demonstrate that during the global financial crisis (GFC) and zero lower bound (ZLB) era, fiscal erraticism operated primarily as a real-economy friction, suppressing industrial production and employment while nominal prices remained anchored. However, in the high-debted COVID epoch, this transmission mechanism fundamentally fractured. Fiscal confusion now bypasses the real economy, transmitting directly into acute inflationary unmooring and compressions of the sovereign term premium. These findings confirm that in the modern era of elevated sovereign debt, fiscal forward guidance is no longer mere political noise; it is a primary driver of financial instability and nominal risk pricing.

title: Integrating Interpretable Multi-modal Machine Learning and Biological Networks Decodes Genotype-Phenotype Maps

detail.title: Integrating Interpretable Multi-modal Machine Learning and Biological Networks Decodes Genotype-Phenotype Maps
detail.abstract: Resolving causal genes from quantitative trait loci (QTL) remains fundamentally limited by linkage disequilibrium. We developed an interpretable machine learning framework that utilizes multi-omic data, which enables it to capture higher-order nonlinear genotype-phenotype relationships and allows conditional evaluation of genetic variants, enabling statistical decorrelation of linked loci. Applied to Saccharomyces cerevisiae segregants across chemical stress conditions, our models, built by integrating genomics and phenomics data, achieved >75% prediction accuracy and identified known causal genes, including MKT1 (genotoxic stress) and IRA2 (osmotic stress). SHAP-based analysis recovered 56% of the validated pleiotropic genes, compared with 36% by conventional contingency testing. Integration with genome-scale metabolic models built using transcriptomic data revealed pathway enrichments distinguishing high-growing strains, including carbon transport, glycolysis, and oxidative phosphorylation. Notably, gene regulatory network analysis identified a novel function for PDR8 in protein mannosylation and cell wall integrity—functions extending beyond its role in drug resistance. This framework demonstrates that interpretable machine learning, coupled with systems biology, transforms QTL associations into mechanistic biological insight.

title: Let's Modify Safety Valve to Value Family Ties

detail.abstract: Federal sentencing law has long struggled to balance the breadth of drug conspiracy liability with the principle of proportional punishment. The statutory "safety valve" provision, codifed at 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f) and mirrored in the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines, was designed to provide relief from mandatory minimum sentences for low-level, nonviolent offenders. Yet its requirement that defendants disclose all information concerning the offense sometimes places familymember codefendants in an untenable position: they may avoid harsh penalties only by incriminating loved ones. The requirement also conficts with other provisions of the Guidelines that provide guidelines reductions, but not relief from mandatory minimum sentences, to individuals motivated by an intimate or familial relationship. This article argues that the current safety valve regime undermines both sentencing fairness and the rehabilitative potential of family relationships by compelling family members to choose between their liberty and their loyalty. Congress and the Sentencing Commission should therefore amend safety valve to exclude disclosures implicating loved ones. Such a modifcation would harmonize federal sentencing law with its own recognition of family ties as a mitigating circumstance, reduce disparities across jurisdictions, and mitigate the collateral damage that drug prosecutions infict on families and communities.

title: Tyranny of the Weak in Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Tyranny of the Weak in Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Bounded rationality can become a source of strength in repeated games. We examine the case in which one player is boundedly rational by being restricted to act through an automaton, while the other player is not and is seen as rational. The constrained player appears disadvantaged, but his automaton structure makes him unable to deviate from declared strategies. Non deviation is formalised as commitment which can coerce the rational player.  We apply the tyranny of the weak framework to the El Farol Bar Problem and use reinforcement learning to run simulations that explore the influence of automata on the ecology of a multi-agent dynamic system. Finally, we describe and simulate the application of tyranny of the weak as a method to train self driving cars as rational agents to react to pedestrians formalised as automata, which are classified on different cognitive hierarchies.

title: Sentiment and Shock Transmission across European Equity Markets
affiliations: University of Padua - Department of Economics and Management , , University of Padua and

detail.title: Sentiment and Shock Transmission across European Equity Markets
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether investor sentiment amplifies the transmission of systemic risk across European equity markets. We study six major benchmark indices-France, Germany, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom-over the period from January 2011 to December 2023. To capture the behavioural dimension of market integration, we construct country-level sentiment indices from abnormal trading activity, volatility premium, and consumer confidence, and aggregate them into a composite European sentiment factor. We then estimate time-varying equity-market connectedness, decompose it across investment horizons, and assess the sentiment-connectedness nexus through a quantile-on-quantile framework. The results point to four main findings. First, European equity markets are persistently highly connected, indicating that cross-border spillovers are a structural feature of the regional financial system. Second, connectedness increases during major stress episodes, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, and remains elevated during the Russia-Ukraine war period. Third, crisis-related spillovers are driven primarily by the short-term component, suggesting that contagion is transmitted rapidly rather than through slow-moving adjustments. Fourth, the e!ect of sentiment on connectedness is strongly state-dependent: it is limited in normal conditions, but becomes materially stronger when sentiment is extreme and markets are already highly synchronized. Country-level evidence reveals marked asymmetries. Deteriorating sentiment in core markets such as Germany and the Netherlands is associated with stronger pessimistic-tail amplification, whereas euphoric-tail e!ects are more pronounced in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Italy. Spain displays weaker tail e!ects at the main diagnostic points, although isolated extreme configurations remain economically relevant. Overall, the findings suggest that investor sentiment is not a constant driver of European equity-market integration, but a conditional amplification mechanism that becomes most relevant when systemic fragility is already high. This has direct implications for portfolio diversification, market surveillance, and the monitoring of financial stability in integrated market areas.

detail.abstract:
Background: Chronic airways diseases impose substantial clinical and economic burdens in Vietnam. Established treatment algorithms for these conditions require differentiation between asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which can impede timely treatment at the primary care level. The VCAPS4 trial evaluated a simplified anti-inflammatory reliever algorithm using a single inhaler (budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg) for adults presenting with undifferentiated chronic airways disease.

Methods: We conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of the VCAPS4 trial over 12 months compared to usual care from the Vietnamese health system perspective. A total of 3,095 participants were included (control: 1,421; intervention: 1,674). Health outcomes were expressed as exacerbations avoided and quality‑adjusted life‑years (QALYs), calculated using COPD‑specific cost and utility inputs to reflect the dominant pattern of disease severity in the trial population. Sensitivity (deterministic and probabilistic) and scenario analyses were performed.

Findings: Compared with usual care, participants receiving the intervention experienced fewer exacerbations and gained an additional 0.019 QALYs (95% CI: 0.012 to 0.025) over 12 months. The intervention cost INT$210 per exacerbation avoided and was found to be cost saving when taking into the account costs of hospitalisations (INT$-2,342 per QALY). Cost savings were greatest among participants with variable or mixed airflow limitation. Results were robust across sensitivity and scenario analyses.

Interpretation: A simplified single-inhaler approach using budesonide–formoterol was cost-effective for managing undifferentiated chronic airways disease in a resource‑limited primary care setting.

detail.abstract: Background: Computational therapeutic design has advanced rapidly through artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches, yet no standard representation exists for the therapeutic candidate as a structured, computable decision object. Current minimum information standards address experiments (MIAME), models (MI-CLAIM), and assays (MIQE) but not the translational candidate itself. Gap: The absence of a candidate-level representation standard fragments therapeutic design across target biology, molecular optimization, delivery engineering, safety assessment, and regulatory planning. This fragmentation impedes reproducible evaluation, cross-modality comparison, and governed advancement decisions. Contribution: This paper introduces Therapeutic Candidate Decision Records (TCDRs) as computable translational objects and TCDR-MI as a minimum information reporting standard for therapeutic candidate representation. The TCDR schema comprises nine field groups spanning candidate identity, biological mechanism, disease and tissue context, modality details, delivery and biodistribution, manufacturability, safety, evidence gaps, and advancement logic. A multicriteria decision analysis (MCDA) rubric enables structured advancement scoring with explicit sensitivity analysis. Methods: The TCDR schema was derived through a structured four-stage process: (1) systematic enumeration of fields from 14 source standards, frameworks, and regulatory guidance documents; (2) gap analysis identifying translational attributes absent from all surveyed sources; (3) iterative consolidation into nine field groups; and (4) minimum information classification following the MIAME three-tier precedent. A competitive landscape analysis across 25 references confirmed the absence of any comparable standard.

title: The Lazy Miner Hypothesis: Efficiency-Driven Cantillon Effects in Bitcoin
affiliations: University of Vaasa

detail.title: The Lazy Miner Hypothesis: Efficiency-Driven Cantillon Effects in Bitcoin

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that I have no significant competing financial, professional, or personal interests that might have influenced the performance or presentation of the work described in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Richard Cantillon (1680s-1734), an Irish-French economist and early pioneer of political economy, observed that those closest to new money creation gain purchasing power before prices adjust throughout the economy. Bitcoin miners occupy precisely this position as the exclusive first receivers of every newly minted bitcoin. Yet unlike banks in fiat systems, miners cannot retain this advantage indefinitely because the protocol subjects them to relentless competition. This paper proposes the Lazy Miner Hypothesis: when mining profitability deteriorates following halving-induced supply shocks, inefficient operators exit first, generating a predictable sequence of revenue compression, hash rate decline, and subsequent price recovery that redistributes first-receiver gains from weak miners to patient investors. Using daily data from September 2014 to January 2026, a miner stress indicator combining depressed revenue with declining computational commitment predicts 90-day forward returns of 36.5 percentage points after controlling for Federal Reserve policy and energy costs. The coefficient is virtually unchanged when WTI crude oil volatility is added, confirming a protocol-native effect. Horse race regressions show miner stress dominates technical oversold indicators. Placebo tests with randomized halving schedules produce no comparable effects, and forward Sharpe ratios confirm genuine alpha. The premium declines by 12.5 percentage points per halving epoch, consistent with market learning. The approval of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024 significantly diminishes the effect, yet the miner stress signal remains positive and statistically significant, indicating that institutional absorption is underway but incomplete. Bitcoin's competitive mining structure thus transforms Cantillon dynamics from permanent insider advantages into temporary, efficiency-driven rewards that erode as markets mature.

detail.abstract: This study examines the normative trajectory of sexual violence in international criminal law, analyzing its transition from mere "attacks on honor" to major legal classifications such as war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. The objective is to demonstrate how the evolution of international jurisprudence, particularly that of the ad hoc tribunals (ICTY and ICTR), has transformed the legal perception of these acts, making them central elements of systemic macro-criminality. The analysis is based on four theoretical pillars: evolutionary positivism, macro-criminality, the constructivist approach to identity destruction, and the doctrine of due diligence. The results highlight that the classification as "torture" (war crime) now ensures the non-applicability of statutory limitations (imprescriptibility) to these acts, while the classification as a "crime against humanity" reveals their strategic function in the forced displacement of populations. Furthermore, the study highlights the genocidal dimension of rape when used as a weapon of biological and symbolic destruction aimed at the annihilation of a protected group. Finally, the research establishes a direct correlation between state failure and the persistence of impunity. It concludes that the threat of extreme international legal classification remains the most effective lever to compel national authorities to fulfill their responsibility to protect. This reflection calls for increased synergy between academic and judicial institutions to restore effective sovereignty of protection.

title: The Green Paradox: Institutional Plant-Based Policies and the Systemic Waste of Vegetables, Fruits, and Salads in Danish Public Canteens

detail.title: The Green Paradox: Institutional Plant-Based Policies and the Systemic Waste of Vegetables, Fruits, and Salads in Danish Public Canteens
detail.abstract: Plant-based options in canteens and food procurement have become increasingly popular in public institutions in Denmark and the rest of the Nordic region due to the growing momentum of climate targets, and growing societal pressure to eat less meat. This paper questions a structurally important but understudied consequence of this shift, known as the green paradox, whereby the production of vegetables, fruits, salads and starchy staples vastly exceeds diner demand, resulting in systematic plant-based food waste. We evidence that avoidable food waste occurs predominantly from plant-derived foods by mass approximately 30% of all avoidable household food waste is attributed to vegetables and salads alone in Danish households, while school-meal experiments suggest up to 59% in the form of starchy staples in Nordic institutional settings. Meanwhile, the amount of meat wasted is smaller, yet its share of the carbon footprint of waste is disproportionately larger. The paradox arises at the intersection of three dynamics: institutional green signalling through abundant plant-based buffets; a mismatch between menu supply and actual diner preferences; and weak real-time waste tracking by food category. We argue that the supply-side substitution logicreplacing meat with more vegetablescannot succeed without demand-sensitive procurement, portion calibration, and waste measurement transparency. We propose a conceptual smart canteen platform, GreenBalance, integrating real-time waste scales, machine-learning demand forecasting, nudge-based pre-ordering and intrainstitutional surplus redistribution, and outline a four-study empirical research agenda grounded in the Danish context.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether training entrepreneurs to apply systematic approaches to strategic decision-making influences their self-perception of ability. Using a field experiment in which 151 entrepreneurs in Tanzania were randomly assigned to two different versions of entrepreneurial training (an evidence-based vs. a theory-and-evidence-based approach), we find entrepreneurs in the theory-and-evidence-based condition experience a larger and more persistent increase of their self-perception of ability to deal with challenges compared to the evidence-based condition. Additionally, entrepreneurs across the two conditions respond differently to the training depending on their initial levels of perceived ability. By integrating insights from social cognitive psychology, this study contributes to research on entrepreneurial experimentation by uncovering the effect of strategic decision-making training on individuals themselves, not just their ventures' outcomes. Managerial summary Entrepreneurs' self-perceptions of ability are critical for how they engage with learning opportunities and respond to challenges that arise as they develop their businesses. To explore how different versions of training on strategic decision-making impact entrepreneurs' self-perceived abilities to deal with such challenges, we conducted a field experiment with Tanzanian agribusiness entrepreneurs. Results show entrepreneurs who learn to develop a theory-of-value before engaging in experimentation experience a larger increase in self-perceived ability compared to those who experiment without such a theory-of-value, and this effect persists for longer. Our results have practical value for entrepreneurs and support organizations offering training programs and point to self-perception of ability as an important factor to help entrepreneurs follow the behavioral advice they receive during those trainings.

title: Telehealth’s Double-Edged Sword: Hidden Costs of Expanding Access to Virtual Care
affiliations: Miami Herbert Business School, University of Miami, University of Miami - Department of Management Science, University of Miami and University of Miami

detail.title: Telehealth’s Double-Edged Sword: Hidden Costs of Expanding Access to Virtual Care
detail.abstract: Telehealth visits are widely recognized for their capacity to improve patient access to care. However, less is known about how already overworked physicians are adapting to this increased demand, particularly against the backdrop of an ongoing physician shortage. Our study investigates the impact of telehealth adoption on physician workload and the resulting implications for physician burnout and healthcare revenues. We analyze approximately 4 million activity records from 467 physicians across three departments (General Medicine, Neurology, and Dermatology) of a major U.S. healthcare system between 2019 and 2023. Leveraging granular variation in telehealth adoption, we use a difference-indifferences approach to compare high-and low-adopting physicians. We find that telehealth adoption resulted in a substantial expansion of physicians' patient panel; yet, surprisingly, this growth occurred without an increase in visit volume. Our analysis uncovers the likely mechanisms underlying this shift: physicians reallocated visit slots from follow-ups and procedures to new patient consultations and increasingly managed follow-ups through asynchronous messaging. These findings suggest that while telehealth expanded patient access, it also substantially increased physicians' workload and reshaped their clinical workflows. Our subsequent analyses indicate that this additional workload may have contributed to physician burnout and attrition. Moreover, the shifts in clinical workflows contributed to substantial revenue losses for the healthcare organization. Telehealth's potential to expand patient access may come at the cost of increased workload and shifts in physician workflows. These changes can contribute to physician burnout and attrition as well as revenue losses for healthcare organizations. Healthcare organizations should develop strategies to manage the increased workload and also reconsider physician compensation models to better align individual incentives with organizational goals. Meanwhile, policymakers should revise reimbursement models to adequately compensate telehealth services, including asynchronous messaging. Without such reforms, the long-term sustainability of telehealth may be at risk.

title: Untangle Air Connectivity and Tourism Development in China's Domestic Market
affiliations: and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Untangle Air Connectivity and Tourism Development in China's Domestic Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines how domestic air connectivity shapes spatial patterns of tourism development in China. We construct a Domestic Airport Connectivity Index (DACI) at the city level for 2000-2024 and employ an instrumental variable strategy to address potential endogeneity, using the interaction between high-speed rail (HSR) expansion and proximity to hub airports as an instrument. The results show that stronger air connectivity significantly boosts tourism development. A one-unit rise in DACI is associated with a 36.5% increase in arrivals and a 61% increase in revenue, which corresponds to 9.5 million additional tourists and 17 billion CNY in additional revenue per city-year. These findings highlight the disproportionate contribution of air travel to higher-value tourism demand. More broadly, the results indicate that aviation plays a unique and complementary role alongside HSR in facilitating domestic mobility and supporting tourism flows across regions. This study contributes by introducing a network-based measure of domestic air connectivity, providing causal evidence of its impact on tourism, and offering new insights from China's dual aviation-HSR transport environment. The results underscore the importance of aviation policy as a lever for promoting tourism development and balanced regional growth.

title: Ethical and Human-Rights Constraints on AI-Assisted Decision-Making: The Dignity-and-Autonomy Test as an Interpretive Layer across CRPD, ICCPR, and the Victorian Charter
affiliations: Independent Researcher, Melbourne, Australia

detail.title: Ethical and Human-Rights Constraints on AI-Assisted Decision-Making: The Dignity-and-Autonomy Test as an Interpretive Layer across CRPD, ICCPR, and the Victorian Charter
detail.abstract:
Public authorities in health, social security, child protection, and custodial settings increasingly rely on

algorithmic inputs — risk-assessment scores, triage classifiers, benefit calculators — when taking decisions that deprive persons of liberty, impose compulsory treatment, or withdraw essential services. Existing human-rights instruments already supply substantive constraints on such decisions; what has been missing is an operational specification of how those constraints apply when the decision-making chain is mediated by an algorithm that is, by design, opaque to the person it affects.

This paper argues that AI ethics discourse functions as an interpretive layer upon — not a parallel framework beside — the dignity, autonomy, liberty, equality, and procedural-fairness guarantees already embedded in the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), and the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (Vic). The operative vehicle is the Dignity-and-Autonomy Test: a three-limb standard requiring, in any rights-engaging algorithmically assisted decision, 

(1) that the affected person can comprehend, in an accessible form, what the system is doing and how

it bears on them; (2) that before any irreversible step the person has a genuine, time-adequate opportunity to consent, refuse, or invoke human review; and (3) that a clearly named human authority remains identifiable and reachable for recourse.

These three limbs operationalise, respectively, obligations in CRPD Articles 12, 14, and 25; ICCPR Article 9; and Charter ss 21, 24, 25(2)(b), and 38. A non-discrimination corollary completes the framework: where an algorithm produces disparate impact on protected groups, the State bears a reverse evidentiary burden to demonstrate necessity, proportionality, and demonstrated ex-ante and ex-post bias auditing under CRPD Articles 5 and 12,

Charter s 8, EO Act s 8, and DDA s 6. The paper maps each failure mode to its optimal forum, applies the test through an anonymised composite compulsory-treatment scenario under the MHWA 2022 (Vic), and surveys remedies from declaratory relief to systemic algorithmic moratoriums. The contribution is to close the AI- governance gap not by waiting for dedicated legislation, but by specifying how courts, tribunals, and regulators must read existing rights guarantees when a public authority relies on an algorithmic input.

detail.title: Beyond Interchange Fee Caps: Rethinking Merchant Choice and Competition in European Payments
detail.abstract: This article examines the persistent challenges in European payment markets a decade after the EU Interchange Fee Regulation. Despite fee caps on debit and credit card transactions, merchants continue to face limited choice and high, often opaque costs, as international card schemes raise non-regulated fees and consumer reliance on cash diminishes. We argue that regulation focused solely on price caps has proven insufficient to address structural imbalances at the point of sale and, possibly to a lesser extent, in e-commerce. While we also set out proposals for adjusting fee regulation, the core of our analysis is a shift in policy towards strengthening merchants' effective choice of payment instruments. Two complementary approaches are developed: first, enabling merchants to initiate direct debit transactions directly from payment card data, thus creating a genuine outside option that disciplines card-based fees; second, breaking single-homing of cardholders by requiring banks to issue multiple branded debit cards or by preventing (quasi-)exclusive issuing arrangements. We also explore tentative remedies in e-commerce and mobile payments, where merchants may, on the one hand, enjoy a wider choice, but digital wallets and intermediaries may also create new "must-have" bottlenecks. Overall, the paper advocates structural reforms to restore competition rather than relying exclusively on fee regulation.

As consumer smartphones evolve from single-shot inference devices into 24/7 Mobile AGI terminals, sensors, ISP, NPU, memory, package interconnects, and power management are no longer merely performance components; they become the physical basis for human oversight, privacy protection, and safe interruption. This paper proposes a mobile-device physical-layer security framework constrained by power, cybersecurity, and regulation, as a consumer-device companion to the 6G fronthaul TGO white paper (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20328129).

The architecture contains three core layers. L1, Topological Geometric Offload (TGO), uses high-dimensional geometric priors and an Mproj: ℝN → ℝ3 mapping to reduce Leq variation in phone-package and sensor-interconnect paths. L2, orthogonal out-of-band transient perturbation ζ(t), provides a local tuning path for package thermal dynamics and dielectric continuity. L3, the Zeno-Triggered Joule Latch (ZTJ-L), is treated as an irreversible or semi-permanent hardware root of trust that can provide a forensic end-state Fend under specified unauthorized sensing, thermodynamic abnormality, or latency-race imbalance conditions.

ZTJ-L (Zeno-Triggered Joule Latch), ECM (Environmental Entropy Coupling), SII (Spatial Inertial Phase Identification), CVD (Causal Vacuum Detection), and Fend (Forensic End-State) are introduced as audit-framework terminology and are first defined here in the academic record.

SII supports detection of fake base stations, phishing channels, and physical-source inconsistencies. CVD checks whether logical data events are decoupled from thermal, electrical, or I/O events. These mechanisms do not replace cryptography or software security; they fill a physical-evidence gap left by software logs, blacklists, and content classifiers under AGI-generated fraud.

detail.title: Mergers, Innovation Efficiencies, and the Investment Channel
detail.abstract: We study how mergers affect innovation and buyer surplus when suppliers invest before competing for a contract awarded to the best supplier. The merger's effect on innovation decomposes into a Schumpeterian effect (larger profit base) and an Arrowian effect (lost rivalry). Without synergies, these cancel exactly: the merger is innovation neutral and harms the buyer by the merger premium. Private and social investment incentives are aligned, so merger-specific synergies always increase total welfare. However, the buyer benefits only indirectly, through competitive pressure the stronger merged entity exerts on outsiders, and only if the innovation gain exceeds the merger premium. In the presence of external spillovers the merger can be more detrimental to welfare. A joint venture that coordinates investment while preserving competition avoids the premium and, in our numerical analysis, benefits the buyer more than the merger across all specifications.

detail.abstract: This study examined the effects of audit committee characteristics on integrated reporting of a selected group of listed non-financial companies in Nigeria. The study specifically looked at how integrated reporting quality was affected by audit committee size, meetings, independence, and financial expertise. The study used a descriptive survey research approach, and 230 respondents-top management personnel, accountants, and internal auditors of selected companies were given standardized questionnaires to complete in order to gather data. Using SPSS version 25, multiple regression analysis and descriptive statistics were used to evaluate the data at the 5% significance level. The study's empirical findings were strengthened and given more contextual support by including the SWOT and PESTEL assessments. The audit committee size has a little but significant influence on integrated reporting, as per the regression results (R = 0.145, R² = 0.021, p = 0.028). Audit committee meetings (p = 0.308), audit committee independence (p = 0.550), and audit committee financial expertise (p = 0.129) had no significant effect on integrated reporting. Additionally, the combined impact of all audit committee attributes did not exhibit statistical significance (R 2 = 0.039, p = 0.059). The study comes to the conclusion that integrated reporting quality cannot be much improved by audit committee features alone. It is recommended that businesses increase the efficacy of their audit committees by providing ongoing training, enhancing their independence, integrating them with corporate reporting frameworks, environmental, social, and governance (ESG), and emphasizing performance-based governance over structural compliance.

title: Dynamic Consistency in Cumulative Stage-weighting Rules

detail.title: Dynamic Consistency in Cumulative Stage-weighting Rules
detail.abstract: Many multi-stage competitions aggregate per-stage scores using cumulative weights that change at each stage boundary. We formulate a dynamic-consistency requirement for cumulative stage weighting and characterise the class of weighting schemes that satisfy it. A scheme is dynamically consistent if and only if it is order-equivalent to a fixed-stage-weight cumulative sum. This identifies the design class of cumulative weighting schemes that aggregate completed stages without rewriting their relative standing. Any violation admits score profiles at which the ordering on already-observed data is reversed at the stage transition, before any new performance is recorded. The scheme used in the 19th International Chopin Piano Competition (2025) violates the property at both non-trivial transitions; using the official rounded raw stage averages, the Stage 3 → Final re-weighting would swap the contestants ranked 10th and 12th at the top-eleven boundary. The pathology lies in the weighting layer and is independent of any score-correction rule.

detail.abstract:
Transportation electrification is expected to become a major source of long-run electricity-demand growth in the United States at a time when the electric grid is already facing mounting pressure from AI-driven data-center expansion, domestic manufacturing reshoring, and broader economy-wide electrification trends. These converging demand pressures carry important implications for electric-grid infrastructure, utility planning, transmission investment, and automotive-sector investment. Yet most existing electric-vehicle (EV) forecasts operate primarily at the national level, offering limited guidance for state-level and regional infrastructure planning despite substantial cross-state heterogeneity in EV adoption patterns and electricity-demand impacts.

This paper develops a national- and state-level framework for forecasting light-duty battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption and associated electricity demand across all 50 US states and the District of Columbia from 2026 to 2040. The framework combines a national Bayesian logistic diffusion model with state-specific adoption ceilings estimated through an ensemble regression incorporating charging-infrastructure density, urbanization, gasoline prices, household income, and ZEV-mandate status, linked to a bottom-up vehicle-category electricity-demand model. Three scenarios (conservative, base, accelerated) bracket the range of plausible long-run adoption outcomes.

Under the base scenario, the stock-weighted US average BEV new-car sales share rises from 8.04% in 2025 to 26.1% by 2030 and 49.4% by 2040. The analysis identifies a persistent divergence between ZEV-mandate and non-mandate states, with the adoption gap widening from +5.4 percentage points in 2025 to +31.5 percentage points by 2040 (63.5% versus 32.0%). State-level projections span 87.0% (California and Washington) to 10.1% (West Virginia). Light-duty BEV adoption alone is projected to increase annual U.S. electricity demand by approximately 61 TWh in 2030 and 326 TWh in 2040. Relative to 2025 U.S. retail electricity sales (4,058 TWh), the 2040 increase is equivalent to roughly 8.04% additional demand. Across scenarios, the estimated incremental demand in 2040 ranges from 246 to 397 TWh. State-level BEV-driven electricity-demand growth ranges from +26.19% (California) to +0.93% (West Virginia), representing an approximately 28x spread across jurisdictions. The framework also projects cumulative new light-duty BEV sales of approximately 83.23 million units in the United States between 2026 and 2040 under the base scenario.

These findings suggest that nationally aggregated EV-adoption assumptions may obscure materially different infrastructure requirements across states and regional utility systems. The framework developed in this paper provides a transparent and reproducible approach for analyzing the geographic distribution of transportation electrification and its implications for transmission planning, distribution-system reinforcement, charging-infrastructure deployment, and long-horizon utility and automotive-sector investment decisions.

title: When Code Meets Custody: How the Proposed CLARITY Act and Ondo Finance Are Reshaping Securities Tokenization
