detail.abstract:
The contemporary debate over AI governance is organized along a single axis: public ownership of foundation-model infrastructure (the public-AI position; Vipra and Korinek 2023; Mazzucato 2015) versus private oligopoly with the techno-feudalism critique as a limit case (Varoufakis 2023; Durand 2024). Korinek and Vipra (2025) prove that under bundled access and quality-recursion returns to scale (Λ > 1), foundation-model markets tip to monopoly. This paper supplies the constructive counterpart: under structural decoupling on a three-component access vector μ = (ω, π, ν) (weight openness, compute portability, verification unbundling), tipping fails to fire and ownership type θ becomes welfare-second-order.

The argument runs through five theorems. (T1) An Access-Structure Separation Theorem (characterization form): θ ⊥_W μ iff the regulatory regime is ownership-invariant, with four sufficient mechanisms (M_α)–(M_δ); this generalizes the privatization-neutrality literature (Sappington and Stiglitz 1987; White 1996; Matsumura 1998; Tomaru 2025) on three axes simultaneously — vector-μ access structure replaces scalar θ, the four mechanism families are unified under a single decomposition, and the result is chained to the natural-monopoly Λ > 1 regime via T3. (T2) A Monopolization Inequality Bound on mean log deviation, GE_0* − GE_0^(0) ≤ κ_1 s_K(η)(1−μ) + κ_2 R̃(ν), with capital-rent and certification-rent channels bounded separately, and a Gini corollary under Lerman and Yitzhaki (1985) comonotonicity. (T3) An Anti-Tipping Theorem with closed-form effective scale exponent Λ^eff(ω, π, ν) = δ(1−ω) + (β+γ) r(ω, π, ν) on Korinek and Vipra (2025)'s technology specification, yielding a single-lever sufficient condition ω > (Λ − 1)/[δ + (β+γ) w_p] that identifies weight openness as the sharpest policy variable in the moderate-Λ, moderate-w_p regime; at large Λ or low w_p a multi-lever bundle is required. (T4) A Verification-Binding Theorem on the credence-good portion of the foundation-model output space, derived from Darby and Karni (1973), Lizzeri (1999), and Klein and Leffler (1981): there exists c > 0 independent of (ω, π) such that W*(ω, π, ν) − W*(ω, π, 0) ≥ c·ν (welfare gain from ν-unbundling is linear in ν at first order). The credence-good gap independence is proved as a derived lemma. (T5) A Long-run Orthogonality Theorem via Stigler–Peltzman–Becker capture-game (Peltzman 1976; Becker 1983; Grossman and Helpman 1994; Laffont and Tirole 1991) showing the static result survives political-economy feedback under regulatory commitment plus rent-zero + IC-financing implementation; the result extends to multi-agency regulation under the Laffont and Tirole (1991) dual-regulator extension.

We validate against a 2×2 case grid (Soviet Gosplan, Saudi Aramco, Norway, Linux, OpenAI–Anthropic–Google trio, Bell System, China Mobile pre- and post-2008). The empirical record is consistent with the credence-good access channel but does not isolate it from six institutional-economics rivals (institutional-origins, resource-curse, first-mover, common-law, Cold-War, trust-radius); discriminating tests require infrastructure not yet built. Three policy mechanisms (compute portability modelled on 47 U.S.C. §251(b)(2) telecom number portability; open-weights minimum disclosure modelled on Hatch–Waxman 21 U.S.C. §355(j); verification unbundling modelled on NRSRO licensing 15 U.S.C. §78o-7) are structurally invariant to ownership type. The verification-unbundling proposal draws the cautionary lesson from the 2008 GFC NRSRO failure (White 2010; Mathis et al. 2009): we treat NRSRO as counter-example, not exemplar, and derive five capture-resistance constraints (C1)–(C5) from its specific failure modes. The paper engages the antimonopoly counter-position of Narechania and Sitaraman (2024) directly: the Networks–Platforms–Utilities toolkit is an implementing instrument for components of μ, not a free-standing alternative to access regulation.

detail.abstract: New TIAA Institute-GFLEC research reveals that workers' expectations about how long they'll live in retirement directly influence their saving and planning behavior. Yet many Americans lack longevity literacy—the understanding of how long people typically live after reaching retirement age—putting their retirement security at risk. This fourth report in the Personal Finance (P-Fin) Index longevity series demonstrates that workers who anticipate longer retirements are significantly more diligent about retirement planning and saving than those expecting shorter retirements. Only 48% of workers expecting fewer than 10 years in retirement save regularly, compared to 71% of those anticipating 30 or more years. These expectations are strongly shaped by workers' perceptions of typical life expectancy at age 65—yet only 33% of U.S. adults can correctly identify this, while 32% underestimate it and 22% admit they don't know. This poor longevity literacy creates a critical retirement security challenge: workers who underestimate typical lifespans plan with horizons that are effectively "too short," save less diligently, and risk having inadequate financial resources during what may prove to be a lengthy retirement.

detail.abstract: Employers offering defined contribution (DC) plans have the option to provide traditional tax-deferred accounts, Roth accounts, or both. Traditional accounts provide deferral of contributions and asset earnings, with distributions fully taxable. By comparison, Roth contributions are not deducted from current taxable income, and withdrawals (including asset earnings) are tax-free. In this study, we analyze the characteristics of workers who are Roth contributors within a TIAA record kept plan. Among actively contributing participants, 42% had a Roth account option in their retirement plan. We find 12% of participants use a Roth option. Utilization of a Roth option depends on age, default status, plan contribution requirements, and whether a Roth option was available when joining the plan. We find evidence of contribution inertia, with participants who did not have a Roth option when joining the plan being less likely to have Roth contributions. Participants who are younger, not plan investment defaulters, and in a DC plan with mandatory employee contributions are significantly more likely to locate contributions to a Roth account. Half of Roth contributors use Roth accounts exclusively. Roth-contributing participants save more on a tax-equivalent basis except when they have mandatory contributions. Our results provide insight into how plan design impacts household tax location decisions and provides insights into how retirement policy changes may affect household retirement security.

title: Modern U.S. Industrial Policy as Economic Security
affiliations: Council on Foreign Relations and

detail.title: Modern U.S. Industrial Policy as Economic Security
detail.abstract:
Industrial policy has returned to the United States in full force. Three administrations have implemented new policy frameworks to shape the future of the U.S. economy through government intervention. However, while industrial policy under two different presidents—Donald Trump and Joe Biden—has largely been driven by similar overarching goals, their approaches to achieving the objectives of revitalizing the U.S. industrial base, competing against geopolitical rivals, and leveraging allies to support U.S. hegemony have varied. Despite that variation, U.S. industrial policy evolved considerably from the first to the second Trump administration. While the underlying motivations may have remained broadly consistent, the broadening of the industrial policy toolkit in each successive administration reflects a process of learning and political adaptation.

 The three phases of modern U.S. industrial policy can best be described as experimental, everything bagel, and imperial. The first Trump administration employed a range of tools, but had no overarching strategy; the Biden administration employed a traditional toolkit, relying predominantly on legislation, but had wide-ranging objectives that sometimes worked at cross-purposes; and the second Trump administration has so far overseen a more robust executive promoting aggressive government interventions in private markets. Neither administration has directly acknowledged the tradeoffs involved in their specific interventions. While many of the policies of the second Trump administration remain to be seen, the patterns that have emerged in the last year present a significant evolution of U.S. industrial policy that leans more heavily on the executive branch. This carries significant consequences for the future of American industrial strategy, as well as U.S. foreign economic relations.

detail.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines are increasingly deployed as the decision-making core of autonomous anti-money laundering (AML) agents in production financial institutions. Unlike stateless classifiers, these agents maintain a persistent vector memory that conditions every downstream compliance decision. We demonstrate that this architectural feature introduces a critical attack surface: adversarial memory injection, whereby an attacker influencing documents ingested into the agent's memory can systematically degrade risk-scoring accuracy and suppress suspicious activity report (SAR) generation. We formalise this threat as the Compliance Memory Poisoning Problem (CMPP) and characterise three injection vectors on a synthetic AML corpus derived from the PaySim simulator. Our most striking finding is that query-time prompt injection (QTPI) collapses agent F1 from a baseline of 0.919 to 0.014 at an injection budget of just 50 documents-a 98.4% degradation rendering the agent operationally equivalent to random guessing. Document-level corpus poisoning and retrieval-rank manipulation show high resistance (F1 ≥ 0.924) under heuristic classification, a finding we interpret as evidence of strong keyword-based priors and a critical motivator for LLM-backend evaluation. In response, we design the Memory Hygiene Layer (MHL)-a modular, training-free defense comprising cryptographic provenance tracking (CPT), cross-encoder factual consistency scoring (FCS), and statistical retrieval anomaly detection (SRAD). CPT achieves 100% adversarial document detection with 0% false quarantine rate; FCS introduces effective semantic filtering at 22.6 ms p99 latency, with threshold calibration required to control false quarantine (30.4-59.8% depending on threshold). These findings directly inform FINRA 2026 agentic AI governance requirements and FCA traceability standards.

detail.abstract: As a part of a special issue that includes several contributions presenting national findings in regional clusters, this paper examines the notions of the average and vulnerable consumer in Turkish and Serbian case law. The case law analysis shows, among other things, that courts and administrative authorities recognize that the average consumer does not read contracts thoroughly, does not master foreign languages, and has a rather limited attention span.  Serbian competent authority does not impose higher expectations on the average consumer, whereas Turkish law does present several instances of such slightly higher standards, where courts place the duty to conduct thorough research on the consumers of certain products. A similarly higher threshold is adopted in trademark cases as the average consumer of a more expensive or essential product or service is expected to be more cautious and sophisticated. Turkish administrative authorities also treat several online interface designs as unfair commercial practices, particularly where consumers are nudged into unintended choices through pre-ticked options, automatic subscription renewals following “free trials,” or hidden additional charges. On the other hand, certain contracts are considered to exclude the possibility of a consumer transaction regardless of how the consumer involved may hold the features of an average consumer. So far, Serbian case law has not shown an inclination to impose these higher standards. The inadequate application and understanding of basic consumer law concepts are most evident in the context of the vulnerable consumer. Case law in both countries appears to avoid assessing this legal standard.

detail.title: Introducing DURPIN: A Diagnostic Performance Ratio based on Firm-specific Risk
detail.abstract: This article introduces the Derived Unsystematic Risk Performance Index (DURPIN) as a complementary diagnostic measure for evaluating excess return generated per unit of estimated unsystematic risk. Conventional performance measures such as the Sharpe Ratio, Treynor Ratio, and Jensen’s Alpha provide important insights into total-risk-adjusted, systematic-risk-adjusted, and abnormal return-based performance. Similarly, the Appraisal Ratio relates alpha to residual or non-systematic risk. However, many individual investors and financial advisors deal with concentrated equity positions where firm-specific risk is not fully diversified away in practice. DURPIN is proposed to address this practical setting by relating realized excess return, measured as stock return minus the risk-free rate, to the estimated unsystematic-risk component of the stock. The study applies DURPIN to selected Indian and US stocks to illustrate how the measure may complement established performance ratios in evaluating firm-specific risk-return efficiency across normal and crisis-related market conditions. The findings suggest that DURPIN may provide useful additional insight for retail investors, financial advisors, sectoral portfolios, thematic investments, and concentrated equity holdings. The paper positions DURPIN not as a replacement for existing models but as a simple practitioner-oriented tool for interpreting excess return relative to unsystematic risk actually retained by investors.

title: Fiscal Architecture For A Just Society: A Comprehensive Tax and Revenue Policy Paper

detail.title: Fiscal Architecture For A Just Society: A Comprehensive Tax and Revenue Policy Paper
detail.abstract:
This paper presents a comprehensive federal tax and revenue architecture designed to fund a unified social safety net—Universal Basic Income, Universal Retirement Income, Universal Healthcare, and related programs—while improving the long-term federal fiscal position. The proposal consists of:

(1) a 17-bracket progressive income tax (10–90%) with consistent 5-percentage-point increments and growing bracket widths, replacing the current seven-bracket structure;

(2) parallel capital gains brackets with mark-to-market taxation of unrealized gains, eliminating the deferral-and-step-up advantage created by the realization requirement;

(3) a marginal wealth tax on household assets above approximately $1.5 million, capped at 10%; and

(4) supporting reforms including a strengthened exit tax, an employer healthcare payroll tax, and graduated estate and inheritance taxation.

Every threshold—bracket boundaries, benefit levels, wealth tax bands, estate exemptions—is indexed to the federal poverty guideline, eliminating the legislative-lag problem that plagues current statutory thresholds. The paper presents transparent walk-forward arithmetic showing total proposed spending of approximately $12.2 trillion against projected revenue of $10.3–11.5 trillion, with three scenarios incorporating behavioral and interaction discounts. A structural market-balance argument demonstrates that wealth-tax-driven asset sales (estimated at $300–500 billion annually) are exceeded by automatic Universal Retirement Income investment buying ($750 billion annually), producing net buying pressure rather than market disruption. Bedrock resilience mechanisms insulate essential programs from the volatility of mark-to-market and wealth tax revenue. Under central assumptions, the architecture fully funds over $6 trillion in new programs while reducing the federal deficit by approximately $1 trillion during transition and substantially more at steady state.

detail.abstract: We propose a non-probabilistic model of state-space expansion integrating unawareness-structure and growing-awareness approaches. Subjective state spaces are interpreted as framework-based projections of an objective state. In contrast to reverse-Bayesian updating models that emphasize probabilistic consistency over previously conceivable events,  our framework captures the rejection of prior interpretive structures triggered by new logical constraints. Awareness expansion is formalized as a response to cognitive dissonance between predicted and realized outcomes. Under finiteness assumptions, the process stabilizes. The model provides a behavioral foundation for institutional rigidity and non-linear socio-technical transitions.

detail.abstract:
Purpose
This article develops a mechanism-based account of neo-imperialism in contemporary U.S. geostrategy
under the Trump II administration. It argues that hierarchy is pursued through forms of conditional
interdependence in which access to markets, infrastructures, technologies, and strategic networks is
made contingent on alignment, trusted-partner status, and compliance. The article examines how these
mechanisms are articulated through firms and compliance architectures and what this implies for
multinational corporations’ strategy, positioning, and alignment choices, as well as for international
business scholarship.
Design/methodology/approach
The article undertakes a qualitative content analysis of two central U.S. policy documents: the 2025
National Security Strategy and the U.S. Department of State Agency Strategic Plan for 2026–2030.
Using a five-part diagnostic framework, it analyses how the texts articulate regional primacy,
conditional access, network leverage, technology and standards governance, and corporate
mobilisation, and how these mechanisms position firms as channels through which conditional
interdependence is operationalised.
Findings
The analysis identifies a neo-imperial shift from managing geopolitical risk to governing cross-border
economic activity through conditionality, infrastructural gatekeeping, and ecosystem control. The
documents articulate conditional interdependence, in which participation in markets, technologies,
infrastructures, and strategic networks is shaped by political and institutional conditions. Firms are
positioned both as objects of discipline and redesign and as agents of implementation that reproduce
hierarchy through standards, compliance, localisation, procurement, and ecosystem alignment.
Strategic choice for U.S. and non-U.S. firms is structured around recurring trade-offs between
alignment and hedging, integration and duplication, and state-embedded and market-led expansion.
Originality
The article develops an account of infrastructural neo-imperialism organised through conditional
interdependence, in which firms, networks, and compliance architectures function as mechanisms for
governing access, exclusion, and alignment. It advances international business research by moving
beyond exogenous geopolitical risk to explain how hierarchy is produced and reproduced through
corporate organisation, network control, and politically governed interdependence.

title: Small States and the Post-Brexit Franco-German Dynamic: Assessing Power, Strategy, and Adaptation in the EU

detail.title: Small States and the Post-Brexit Franco-German Dynamic: Assessing Power, Strategy, and Adaptation in the EU

detail.abstract:
The withdrawal of the United Kingdom from the European Union represents one of the most significant transformations in the history of European integration, reshaping institutional dynamics, political equilibria, and the distribution of influence among member states. The absence of a traditional veto player, Atlanticist voice, and liberal counterweight reopened longstanding debates on the nature and viability of Franco-German leadership in the Union. While initial assessments suggested that Brexit would strengthen Paris and Berlin's agenda-setting capacity, closer analysis reveals a more complex and often contradictory reality. 

Brexit has also intensified the vulnerabilities of smaller EU member states. Long constrained by structural disadvantages in bargaining, argumentative, and moral institutional power, their formal leverage has been further reduced by changes to qualified majority voting. Yet small states remain far from passive actors. Through coalition-building, selective policy engagement, diplomatic entrepreneurship, institutional leadership, and norm advocacy, they continue to exert meaningful influence within the EU. 

This article provides a theoretically grounded and empirically informed analysis of the post-Brexit landscape, focusing on Franco-German dynamics, structural constraints on small states, and the distinct strategies adopted by Luxembourg and Malta.

title: Structural Divergence in the EU: Convergence Clubs, Structural Funds, and the Role of Institutional Quality

detail.title: Structural Divergence in the EU: Convergence Clubs, Structural Funds, and the Role of Institutional Quality

declarations.funderStatement: This paper was funded by the European Union NextGenerationEU under Call IIP 581 2025.

detail.abstract: We study the dynamics of regional GDP per capita across 232 EU NUTS 2 regions from 2000 to 2022 and ask whether cohesion policy and institutional quality help lagging regions move toward higher long-run development paths or leave them on lower-income ones. Applying the Phillips and Sul (2007) log t test, we reject absolute convergence across all regions and identify four convergence clubs separated by persistent structural differences in income, employment, population growth, and institutional quality. To explain club membership, we estimate ordered probit models that include regional fundamentals, expenditures from seven EU structural funds disaggregated individually (ERDF, ESF, Cohesion Fund, EAFRD, EMFF, FEAD, and YEI), and a total of eight institutional quality indicators (Index of Economic Freedom, six Worldwide Governance Indicators, and the European Quality of Government Index). Lower-income clubs receive a larger share of EU funding, indicating that allocation is consistent with stated targeting goals. Higher-income clubs are systematically associated with stronger institutional quality. The first and the fourth clubs comprise six and eight regions, respectively. The majority of regions are distributed between the second and third clubs, which together include over 90% of regions. The results describe a structurally divergent EU in which financial transfers alone do not generate convergence and suggest that cohesion policy is most effective when paired with reforms that strengthen institutional performance.

title: Rolling Legendre-Fenchel Rate Functions as Crypto Fragility Diagnostics

detail.title: Rolling Legendre-Fenchel Rate Functions as Crypto Fragility Diagnostics
detail.abstract: Scalar risk measures such as volatility, VaR, and tail-index estimates compress tail behavior into one-dimensional summaries and can obscure the empirical geometry of downside fragility. This paper studies rolling empirical Legendre-Fenchel rate-function surfaces as diagnostic state variables for cryptocurrency tail risk, not as universal event timers. The central object is a fragility coordinate: the minimum exponentialtilting cost needed to make a drawdown-consistent average return plausible in the recent window. On BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT daily data from 2019-2026, this coordinate is most informative for cross-regime separability. For 30-day BTC drawdowns of at least 20%, HDLDR reaches AUC 0.631 versus 0.529 for realized volatility, but the dependence-robust block bootstrap is marginal (p = 0.064 at a 21-day block); the significant DeLong result (z = 4.71, p < 0.001) is therefore treated as a parametric reference rather than the binding inference. Evidence is weaker for ETH and for short horizons, and incremental gains over a multivariate XGBoost benchmark are not robust under block bootstrap. The strongest mechanistic evidence comes from a one-hour Binance Futures liquidation-pressure extension using licensed 2025-2026 records: for 72-hour future liquidation pressure, adding 1h LDT features raises Spearman IC from 0.418 to 0.629 for BTC and from 0.436 to 0.622 for ETH, with positive 336-hour block-bootstrap intervals. Methodologically, a horizonconsistent threshold correction avoids a 26.9× unit mismatch that otherwise makes the BTC estimator non-computable. HDLDR can be calibrated into a valid 99% VaR model, but it does not improve quantile loss relative to Gaussian VaR. Rolling rate surfaces therefore complement, rather than replace, volatility and VaR models.

title: Securing the Supply of Graphite for Batteries

detail.title: Securing the Supply of Graphite for Batteries
detail.abstract: Battery-grade graphite is the highest-volume active material in lithium-ion cells, yet over 92% of global anode-grade production is concentrated in a single country (China), creating a structural vulnerability for energy storage supply chains worldwide. Here we present the first industry-validated, process-based cost models for both natural and synthetic battery-grade graphite. The models are developed through structured input from 120 experts across 70 organizations and we use them to identify the conditions under which supply chain diversification becomes economically viable. We find that production costs in non-Chinese production environments exceed Chinese market prices by 100-200%, with capital costs as the dominant barrier for any new producer entering the market. Our sensitivity analysis identifies financing structures and particle shaping yields as the highest-leverage near-term interventions, together reducing costs by 25–30%, with further process optimizations reaching 35–40%. Critically, even maximizing all conventional improvements leaves costs above current Chinese market prices, underscoring the need for disruptive innovation. We derive explicit cost targets that emerging technologies such as methane pyrolysis, catalytic graphitization, and end-of-life battery recycling must achieve to become viable, providing a quantitative roadmap for R&D investment and supply chain scale-up globally.

title: Machine Verifiable Law in Aerospace and Autonomous Vehicles: A Blockchain-anchored Certification Framework for Safety-critical Autonomous Systems

detail.abstract:
Autonomous vehicles and autonomous aerospace systems are making real time safety critical decisions at machine speed, in operating environments where the consequence of an incorrect decision is measured in human lives.

The regulatory frameworks governing these systems, the FAA's type certification process, NHTSA's Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards, EASA's CS 25 airworthiness criteria, and international standards including DO 178C and ISO 26262, were designed for deterministic, human operated systems and have not been fundamentally restructured to address the epistemic challenge posed by AI driven autonomous decision making: that the system's decision logic cannot be fully inspected, predicted, or verified by the humans who certify it.

title: Deep Learning Segmentation of Enamel Nanoscale Architecture Fromsynchrotron Computed Tomography for Bioinspired Material Design
affiliations: University of Washington, University of Washington, Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory, University of Washington, Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory and University of Washington - Department of Materials Science and Engineering

detail.title: Deep Learning Segmentation of Enamel Nanoscale Architecture Fromsynchrotron Computed Tomography for Bioinspired Material Design
detail.abstract: Tooth enamel achieves an unusual combination of high hardness and exceptional fracture resistance through a hierarchical architecture of hydroxyapatite crystallites organized into an assembly of rods. Although microscale rod orientation has been studied, the nanoscale geometry of individual rods remains poorly resolved due to limitations in conventional imaging and segmentation workflows. This study develops an integrated digital pipeline for quantifying enamel rod morphology across species using synchrotron nano-computed tomography (nano-CT), self-supervised deep learning denoising, and automated segmentation. High-resolution nano-CT volumes of enamel from human, African lion, and wild African dog were reconstructed and denoised using a 2.5-dimensional (2.5D) Noise2Inverse U-Net framework. Then, a five-level 2-dimensional (2D) U-Net was trained on manually annotated slices to generate consistent rod-level segmentations across species. The process improved the signal-to-noise ratio by approximately 1.32× while preserving rod boundaries. Quantitative analysis of enamel rods enabled by this visualization revealed significant interspecies differences in rod area, diameter, circularity, and interrod spacing(ANOVA, p<0.001). Human enamel exhibited the smallest rods and densest packing, whereas the lion enamel possessed the largest rod diameters. Structural motifs of the wild African dog enamel displayed the largest interrod spacing and fully enclosed rod sheaths, which provides mechanistic insight to the species-specific crack growth resistance. The segmented rod geometries were converted into fabrication-ready 3-dimensional (3D) surface mesh files, enabling evaluation of whether naturally occurring rod architectures are manufacturable. Overall, this workflow establishes a generalizable​ deep learning–enhanced nano-CT process for generating refined enamel datasets, which in turn enable cross-species comparison of nanoscale rod architecture and inform bioinspired material design.

detail.abstract:
Background: Major depressive disorder (MDD) represents a leading cause of global disability, yet prevalence estimates vary dramatically across countries. While individual-level risk factors are well-documented, the role of structural and socioeconomic determinants in explaining cross-national variation remains poorly understood. The present systematic review and meta-analysis aim to estimate pooled global prevalence of MDD, and evaluate the extent to which country-level structural and socioeconomic indicators explain cross-national variation.

Methods: MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and EMBASE were searched for articles published in English from 2000 to July 2025. Studies were included if they reported lifetime prevalence and/or 12-month prevalence, defined as the proportion of participants meeting criteria for MDD or MDE at any point in the previous 12 months, according to ICD-10, DSM-IV, or DSM-5 criteria; (2) had at least 1,000 participants; and (3) were published in peer-reviewed journals. Study outcomes included lifetime and 12-month prevalence of MDD or MDE. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to estimate pooled prevalence. Mixed-effects meta-regressions examined prevalence moderators.

Outcomes: Forty-four population-based studies, including 60 independent samples from 44 countries across six continents and a total of 1,149,046 participants were included. Pooled lifetime prevalence was 10.2% (95% CI=8.5 to 11.9%) and 12-month prevalence was 4.9% (95% CI=4.2 to 5.6%). For lifetime prevalence, continent explained 47.8% of variance and income level contributed 10.4%, with upper-middle-income countries showing the lowest prevalence. For 12-month prevalence, employment rate was the only significant moderator (β=-0.07, p=0.04) in univariable analyses, with stronger protective effects in Asia (β=-0.29, p<0.01) and Africa (β=-0.23, p=0.04). Continent and income combined explained 60.7% of between-study lifetime variance, while continent and employment explained 30.7% of 12-month variance. Study-level moderators were mostly non-significant.

Interpretation: Structural and socioeconomic determinants partially explain global MDD prevalence, with different factors driving lifetime versus 12-month prevalence, effects varying across continents. Region-specific mental-health strategies should address socioeconomic determinants alongside individual-level interventions.

title: The Persistence of the Wealth Effect: Sovereign Bond Spreads and Climate Transition Risk in the Global South

detail.title: The Persistence of the Wealth Effect: Sovereign Bond Spreads and Climate Transition Risk in the Global South
detail.abstract:
The 2015 Paris Agreement set new expectations for which industries would be profitable
while conforming to climate guidelines. Fossil fuel extraction was not one of them. Bond
markets would react negatively to developing countries discovering oil, as it is a “stranded
asset”. The reaction would take the form of higher rates for the Global South’s sovereign debt.
This paper tests whether the Paris Agreement was a big enough event to disincentivize
investment in oil extraction. Panel data of 21 developing countries from 2000 to 2025 test the
hypothesis. A Two-Way Fixed Effects regression tests whether “giant oil discoveries” have a
higher sovereign borrowing cost in post-2015 vs pre-2015.
The data doesn’t support the main hypothesis. Neither the baseline wealth effect nor the
post-2015 stranded asset penalty is detectable in this sample, suggesting the pre-2015 baseline
may itself have weakened due to partial market discounting of announced discoveries.
Two robustness analyses were conducted: shifting the structural break to 2019, and
removing the largest economy in the dataset (China). Both tests returned null results. The data
suggests that bond markets in the post-2015 era price giant oil discoveries in the global south the
same way they did pre-2015.
The tragedy of the horizon might explain why bond markets fail to price the transition
risk. There is a mismatch between bond maturity cycles (3-10 years) and climate risks that
materialize over 30 years. It seems that sovereign bond indexes cannot internalize long-term risks absent direct regulatory intervention. The mismatch results in a policy implication: developing countries have no disincentive to extract new oil. Without central bank mandates forcing climate risk onto balance sheets, the motivation of extraction will remain.

title: Evolution of Privacy Jurisprudence in the Supreme Court of India: Evaluating the Impact of Puttaswamy

detail.abstract: This paper studies the Supreme Court’s landmark privacy judgment in K.S. Puttaswamy v.Union of India and through an empirical analysis of 53 judgments, analyse the record of the Supreme Court in applying (rather than simply citing) the judgment in decisions from 2017 to early 2023. Puttaswamy is widely seen as a transformative decision as it recognised privacy as a fundamental right and tied it to dignity, autonomy, bodily integrity, consent, and choice. Yet it did not arise from a lis involving a concrete factual dispute over the application of privacy rights. The Court was therefore not dealing with a specific factual matrix, and many questions about the content and limits of privacy were left to be decided by later benches. This paper therefore turns from the promise of Puttaswamy to its actual use in the Supreme Court of India. Based on an empirical review of Supreme Court judgments available on SCC Online, the paper maps the main areas in which privacy claims arose after Puttaswamy and studies what difference the judgment made in practice. These include cases concerning (i) inter-personal relationships, (ii) actions by/against the State, (iii) the intersection between the right to privacy and the right to information, (iv) the application of proportionality and judicial review and (v) pertaining to the interpretation of the Constitution. The paper argues that while Puttaswamy opened up important constitutional possibilities, its promise has been realised unevenly. Its influence has been significant in some areas, limited in others, and still uncertain in many. The paper thus offers an account of what Puttaswamy has changed, and what remains unsettled in Indian constitutional law.

title: Cross-Sector Uncertainty Contagion in the Chinese Equity Market: A Clustered Network Analysis of Climate Policy Shocks

detail.title: Cross-Sector Uncertainty Contagion in the Chinese Equity Market: A Clustered Network Analysis of Climate Policy Shocks
detail.abstract: Identifying the transmission paths of climate transition uncertainty requires separating risk contagion from broad market co-movement. We use the clustered network connectedness framework to do this, applying it to 140 CSI 300 stocks (2018-2023). We partition firms into Brown (high-carbon), Green (low-carbon), and Neutral clusters and use high-frequency realized volatility as the uncertainty proxy. The Brown cluster is a persistent net transmitter of uncertainty (+0.34%), while Green and Neutral clusters are net receivers. The 2020 COVID-19 crash and the 2021 power rationing crisis produced comparable total connectedness, but with opposite transmission structures: COVID was indiscriminate co-movement (Brown net contagion +0.05%), while the energy crisis was a targeted Brown-sector shock (Brown net contagion +0.38%, a sevenfold increase). Green assets are not immune to climate transition risk, as they are exposed to cost shocks from upstream Brown industries through supply chains.

detail.abstract: We test whether emerging-market central-bank gold-reserve accumulation anchors the long-run gold price, on the full 2002–2026 World Gold Council reported-tonnage panel (n = 290 monthly observations). The test families, acceptance criteria, and family-wise Holm corrections were pre-specified in a version-controlled artefact before results were reviewed; the full 2002–2026 WGC window is a data-availability expansion promoted to primary after external review, with the original 2013–2026 window retained as a sub-period robustness. Across pairwise Engle–Granger and Gregory–Hansen cointegration, joint Johansen with an implied-residual stationarity diagnostic, VAR-in-differences under three identifications, multi-lag Granger (SSR-F, Toda–Yamamoto, Breitung–Candelon), regime-conditional Granger, and Welch quartile reflexivity tests, no specification supports the narrative after the pre-specified diagnostic and multiple-testing filters. One readily available alternative panel of "tonnage" series for India and Turkey, sourced from a standard financial-data terminal, recovers an apparent cointegrating slope close to −1 that decomposes algebraically into the deflation arithmetic of dividing a valuation by the gold price; this is a ratio-variable concern (Pearson 1897; Kronmal 1993) that we generalise from cointegration testing to regime classifiers. Monte-Carlo simulations re-run the cointegration, Granger, and regime tests on simulated data with known effect sizes at the primary monthly cadence (T =290): the minimum detectable Granger effect at 50% rejection rate is β_std ≈ 0.12 at one month, rising to ≈ 0.21 at twelve months, with the empirical estimates near zero. The results do not rule out arbitrarily small effects. They do rule against effects large enough to support the practitioner narrative as a tradeable economic relationship.

title: Housing Affordability in Kenya: Key Determinants and Policy Implications

detail.title: Housing Affordability in Kenya: Key Determinants and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: Recent declines in housing affordability and a growing population have sparked renewed interest in research on housing supply. In Kenya, new construction has slowed significantly since the 1970s, with declining housing supply elasticities, especially in densely populated areas. Housing supply constraints and regulations substantially affect prices and affordability. The study is based on the accelerated investment theory, which posits that housing affordability relies on the rate of change in housing demand and income, as well as how quickly developers can adjust supply to meet this demand. This study aims to identify and quantify the factors influencing housing affordability in Kenya using autoregressive distributed lag analysis. The results indicate that housing supply, income levels, and public investment exert significant negative pressure on housing prices, thereby improving affordability, whereas loan interest rates and inflation serve to reduce it. The findings indicate that supply constraints and regulations impact housing prices and affordability. To improve affordability, the Kenyan government should streamline zoning, provide subsidies for low-income households, invest in infrastructure, monitor interest rates, and address construction cost inflation.

title: The Energy–Logistics–Cost Nexus: Assessing LCOE Volatility, Decarbonization Barriers, and SDG 7 Alignment

detail.title: The Energy–Logistics–Cost Nexus: Assessing LCOE Volatility, Decarbonization Barriers, and SDG 7 Alignment
detail.abstract:
As the global energy transition matures, analytical focus has shifted from isolated engineering performance toward integrated system-level economic efficiency. While the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) remains the universal metric for evaluating project viability, traditional models are largely static, failing to incorporate the profound financial impacts of supply chain performance, logistical volatility, and institutional constraints. This study addresses these "integration gaps" by examining the relationship between logistical system conditions, operational disruptions, and sustainability outcomes.

Adopting a critical realist perspective and a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the research utilizes semi-structured interviews with industry experts to identify sources of operational friction, followed by Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and the development of an Integrated LCOE (I-LCOE) model. Central to the study is the Dynamic Logistics–Sustainability Integration Model, which conceptualizes renewable energy systems as interconnected layers where logistical agility directly influences financial risk.

The findings establish logistics as a primary structural cost driver embedded across all project lifecycle phases. The research identifies "logistical velocity" as a critical determinant of the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), as supply chain friction serves as an aggressive risk multiplier that inflates investor risk premiums. Furthermore, physical upscaling of components introduces non-linear logistical constraints that traditional models fail to capture. The study proposes an integrated digital knowledge management platform to resolve information asymmetry. By internalizing traditionally externalized variables such as geopolitical disruptions at maritime chokepoints this research provides a transformative framework for achieving SDG 7 and optimizing the systemic costs of global decarbonization.

title: A Mechanism Design Approach to Multisignal Principal-agent Problems

detail.title: A Mechanism Design Approach to Multisignal Principal-agent Problems
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a  mechanism design approach to validate the first-order approach (FOA) for multisignal principal-agent problems. Traditional validation of the FOA relies on proving the concavity of the agent's payoff through the monotone likelihood ratio property (MLR), combined with the convexity of  the distribution function condition (CDFC) or the concave increasing set probability (CISP). These second-order conditions are frequently violated by many common distributions.  To overcome these limitations, we transform the moral hazard problem into a mechanism design problem by conditioning the wage schedule  on the principal’s recommended action. Parallel to Spence-Mirrlees condition, we show that a wage schedule is incentive compatible if and only if the agent's payoff is supermodular in the principal's recommended action and the agent's action. In addition, the supermodularity of the agent's payoff guarantees that the unimodularity of the agent's payoff in his action. We then identify a  multiplicative-additive form for the likelihood ratio that ensures the supermodularity of the agent's payoff under the optimal contract.  The multiplicative-additive form for the likelihood ratio is applicable to a wide class of distributions, including the exponential family, e.g., Beta, Gamma and multinomial, etc.,  multivariate Normal and log-Normal. Notably, our results remain valid whether the likelihood ratio satisfies either MLR or reverse MLR. Moreover, our approach can aggregate signals from multiple independent sources when the likelihood ratio has a generalized multiplicative-additive form. Finally, we provide an explicit characterization of the optimal contract and the principal’s optimal action choice under both risk neutrality and risk aversion.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the short- and medium-term causal effects of austerity on local fiscal, economic, and political outcomes. We study a 2013 austerity program in Hesse, Germany, coding 2,900 consolidation measures across 86 municipalities and comparing them with 4,630 untreated municipalities using synthetic difference-in-differences. Austerity improves fiscal outcomes through tax increases and spending cuts, but at sizable economic cost: treated municipalities experience slower firm growth, lower salaries, and lower employment. Tax-based adjustment erodes the business tax base and employment, implying higher efficiency costs than expenditure-based consolidation. Political costs arise mainly when consolidation relies heavily on one fiscal instrument.

title: Quantitative Data and Methods for Comparative Immigration Law

detail.title: Quantitative Data and Methods for Comparative Immigration Law
detail.abstract: Over the past years and decades, numerous large-scale quantitative datasets to measure various attributes of immigration law have been generated and analyzed by researchers and teams with wide-ranging and diverse disciplinary backgrounds. Many of them have also employed quantitative methods for descriptive and/or causal analysis to address empirical puzzles emanating from various and often cross-cutting literatures. However, to further propel comparative immigration law forward and to make it a more important and methodologically sophisticated endeavor also for legal scholars, the research community in this field could use an overview of the current data and methods on offer. Against this background, based on the state of the art in quantitative comparative political science, the aim of this Working Paper is to equip students and scholars of other methodological and/or disciplinary backgrounds with the necessary knowledge to be able to understand, assess, and appreciate quantitative research in this area or to join this research enterprise themselves. After describing the constituent domains and the architecture of immigration law, I address the key decisions involved in devising adequate concepts that clearly specify legal attributes of interest for comparative analysis. After a short history of how the measurement of migration-related laws has evolved, the following section explains the measurement methods and then provides an overview of ten existing databases and datasets that can be used to quantify various attributes of immigration law. I then move on to methods for descriptive analysis and methods for causal analysis. I conclude by reflecting on the potentials for interdisciplinary cross-fertilizations between legal scholars and quantitative social scientists in the field of comparative immigration law and its advancement through a common research agenda.

detail.abstract: This master's thesis examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within the context of the digital transformation of multinational enterprises, with particular emphasis on its impact on the speed and operational efficiency of core business processes. As modern organizations operate in an increasingly dynamic and competitive environment, the adoption of advanced technologies has emerged as a critical factor in enhancing organizational performance. The study adopts a qualitative methodological approach and is based on semi-structured interviews conducted with executives from multinational organizations operating in the industrial and technology sectors. Through thematic analysis of the collected data, the research investigates how the integration of artificial intelligence applications affects the execution, coordination, and decision-making processes within business operations. The findings of the study demonstrate that artificial intelligence contributes significantly to reducing process execution time, primarily through the automation of repetitive tasks and the faster processing and analysis of data. At the same time, AI enhances operational efficiency by improving the quality of outcomes, reducing operational errors and redundancies, and optimizing resource utilization. However, the study also highlights that the full realization of AI's potential depends largely on organizational factors such as digital maturity, strategic leadership, and a culture of innovation. Overall, this study contributes to the literature on digital transformation by providing empirical insights into the mechanisms through which artificial intelligence influences organizational speed and operational efficiency, while also offering practical guidance for organizations seeking to strategically leverage its capabilities.

detail.title: From Idea to Exit: An Integrated Framework for Entrepreneurial Viability Assessment, Financial Goal-Setting, and Capital Strategy Across the Startup Lifecycle
detail.abstract: The journey from entrepreneurial idea to viable, fundable, and ultimately exit-ready business remains one of the most consequential and least systematically documented transitions in modern economic life. While the academic literature has addressed individual dimensions of this journey-opportunity recognition, product-market fit, venture capital dynamics, and exit mechanisms-no integrated framework exists that guides entrepreneurs through the complete lifecycle from initial idea validation through Series A growth and onward to exit or business-as-usual (BAU) sustainability. This paper fills that gap by introducing the Idea-to-Exit Framework (IEF), a five-stage integrated model that provides entrepreneurs with a structured architecture for viability assessment, financial metric goal-setting, and capital strategy at each lifecycle stage. The five stages are: (I) Idea Validation, (II) MVP and Market Fit, (III) Early Traction and Seed Readiness, (IV) Growth and Series A, and (V) Scale, Exit, or BAU. For each stage, the IEF specifies: a Viability Gate-the minimum criteria that must be satisfied to proceed; a Financial Metric Dashboardthe specific quantitative indicators that define success at that stage; a Capital Strategy-how much to raise, from whom, at what dilution, and on what terms; and a Stage Exit Condition-the observable signals that indicate readiness to advance. The IEF integrates insights from opportunity recognition theory (Kirzner, 1979; Shane and Venkataraman, 2000), lean startup methodology (Ries, 2011), venture capital decision frameworks (Gompers et al., 2020), and the practitioner-grounded financial metrics documented in the entrepreneurial arithmetic literature (Bollu, 2025d). Validated against 2024-2025 benchmark data from Carta, PitchBook, and NVCA, the IEF provides entrepreneurs with a rigorous, actionable, and empirically grounded roadmap for the full entrepreneurial journey.

title:
From Connectivity to Commerce:
Digital Infrastructure, Rural Entrepreneurship, and the AI Inflection Point
A Comparative Study of India, China, and Southeast Asia

detail.title:
From Connectivity to Commerce:
Digital Infrastructure, Rural Entrepreneurship, and the AI Inflection Point
A Comparative Study of India, China, and Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: Digital infrastructure-internet connectivity, mobile penetration, and now artificial intelligence-is widely cited as a catalyst for rural entrepreneurship in developing economies. Yet the empirical record is sharply heterogeneous: China's Taobao Villages converted rural internet access into a documented ecommerce entrepreneurship phenomenon at massive scale (7,780 villages by 2022), while Southeast Asian economies converted mobile penetration into gig economy participation through super-app platforms. India, despite achieving near-universal mobile broadband affordability (data costs falling from 269/GB in 2014 ₹ to 9.18/GB in 2024) and a stated policy commitment to rural digital empowerment, has not yet produced a ₹ comparable structural transformation of rural entrepreneurial outcomes. This paper introduces the Connectivity-Capability-Commerce (C3) Framework to explain this divergence. The C3 Framework posits that digital infrastructure generates rural entrepreneurial outcomes only when entrepreneurs successfully traverse three sequential layers: Connectivity (access to digital infrastructure), Capability (ability to leverage digital tools for productive economic activity), and Commerce (capacity to generate sustained revenue through digital channels). We argue that the binding constraint on rural entrepreneurship is not the Connectivity layer-which India has largely addressed-but the Capability-to-Commerce transition, which requires platform ecosystems, financial infrastructure, trust mechanisms, and language-accessible tools that have developed differently across the three regions. We further introduce the concept of AI Compression-the mechanism through which generative AI and voice-based AI agents may collapse the Capability layer, enabling a direct Connectivity-to-Commerce transition for rural entrepreneurs who currently lack the digital literacy to traverse Capability independently. Drawing on data from World Bank, TRAI, Alibaba Research Institute, ASEAN Startup White Paper 2024, and Government of India Digital India reports, we provide the most comprehensive comparative analysis to date of how digital infrastructure translates-or fails to translate-into rural entrepreneurial activity across these three regions. The implications are direct for policymakers designing rural development programs, platform companies seeking rural market expansion, and researchers studying the digital economy's distributional effects.

title: Building and Evaluating a Regime-Adaptive Trading Framework for Indian Equities

detail.title: Building and Evaluating a Regime-Adaptive Trading Framework for Indian Equities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently.

detail.abstract:
This paper documents the design, implementation, and backtested evaluation of a modular algorithmic trading system for Indian large-cap equities listed on the NSE. The framework integrates a technical indicator engine, a rule-based market regime classifier, three strategy modules (trend following, momentum, mean reversion), and a fixed-fractional risk management layer. The system is evaluated over a three-year window (January 2021–January 2024) across five Nifty 50 stocks.

The regime-adaptive mechanism classifies market conditions into five states and dynamically routes capital to the most appropriate strategy. Stop-loss conditions are evaluated against intraday lows rather than closing prices for more realistic simulation.

Four of five symbols produced positive nominal returns (+3.54% to +7.65%). HDFCBANK.NS was the exception at -3.31%, tied to its 2022–2023 merger period. All five underperformed the Nifty 50 benchmark (+55%). Maximum drawdowns stayed below 6.1%. Sharpe ratios are negative relative to India's 6.5% risk-free rate — a finding the paper addresses directly.

The framework is not positioned as a production strategy. It is a documented, reproducible system for independent researchers to extend. Limitations including short universe, no walk-forward validation, and rule-based regime classification are discussed in Section 7.

title: Technological Evolution of Hydraulic Injection Molding Machines in Modern Manufacturing Systems

detail.title: Technological Evolution of Hydraulic Injection Molding Machines in Modern Manufacturing Systems

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on secondary market research, publicly available industry data, and business intelligence sources. No human participants, patient data, or confidential personal information were involved; therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Hydraulic Injection Molding Machines (HIMMs) have remained a fundamental technology within the global plastics manufacturing industry due to their high clamping force, operational durability, and suitability for large-scale industrial production. Despite the emergence of electric and hybrid injection molding technologies, hydraulic systems continue to dominate several manufacturing sectors, particularly automotive, packaging, consumer goods, and heavy industrial applications. However, increasing concerns regarding energy consumption, operational efficiency, environmental sustainability, and manufacturing precision have accelerated the technological transformation of injection molding systems through Industry 4.0 integration, automation, and intelligent manufacturing solutions. This paper examines the technological evolution, operational characteristics, and industrial significance of hydraulic injection molding machines while comparatively analyzing hydraulic, electric, and hybrid injection molding technologies. The study further explores the role of advanced control systems, predictive maintenance, energy-efficient technologies, and smart manufacturing frameworks in modern injection molding operations. Additionally, the paper investigates the advantages, limitations, and future industrial prospects of hydraulic injection molding systems in the context of sustainable manufacturing and digital industrial transformation. The findings indicate that although electric and hybrid machines offer improved energy efficiency, precision, and environmental performance, hydraulic injection molding systems continue to maintain competitive advantages in high-force industrial applications due to their durability, lower initial investment costs, and large-scale production capabilities. Furthermore, the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies, artificial intelligence, and intelligent monitoring systems is expected to significantly enhance the operational efficiency and sustainability of hydraulic molding systems in future manufacturing environments.

title:
From Structure to Dynamics: The SMLP Cycle and the SIRC Framework 
A Dynamic Model of Institutional Change and Subject Adaptation

detail.title:
From Structure to Dynamics: The SMLP Cycle and the SIRC Framework 
A Dynamic Model of Institutional Change and Subject Adaptation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Nil

detail.abstract:
Why do governance systems repeatedly fall into the same traps—rigid inertia, fragile stability, and the
domination of subjects by the tools they created? The SIRC framework (Subject, Information, Resources,
Capital) provides a static structural analysis of human civilization: four positions that recur across ten
millennia. But structure alone cannot explain change. This paper proposes the SMLP cycle as the
dynamic complement to SIRC. SMLP describes how subjects (S) use methods (M) to face limitations
(L), adjust purposes (P), and generate new methods (new M). The paper introduces a core distinction
between passive switching (crisis-driven, costly) and active switching (cognition-driven, less costly)
along a spectrum, distinguishing four cognitive sources: strategic, emergent, market-driven, and forced.
Three clusters of historical cases—environmental/resource crises, colonial/imperialist pressures, and
capital/monetary crises—each with four cases, illustrate the switching types and their outcomes. The
paper then develops a typology of inertia: cognitive inertia (not seeing new L) leads to mind
detachment; behavioral inertia (repeating old M) leads to hand detachment; institutional
inertia (institutions acquiring autonomous logic) leads to alienation—the domination of subjects by the
tools they created. Alienation, defined narrowly as domination with no exit, occurs only under
institutional inertia. The paper introduces an erosion chain (Constraint → Optimization → Dependence
→ Institutionalization → Cognitive Lock-in → Alienation → Sovereignty Loss) that traces how
cognitive sovereignty is lost and operationalizes cognitive sovereignty through three dimensions
(epistemic access, institutional space, reflexive capacity). The paper concludes that SIRC is a grammar
of civilizational analysis; SMLP is its narrative. Case details are provided in the Appendix.

title: The Impact of Sovereign Credit Ratings on Foreign Capital Inflows: Evidence from G20 Economies

detail.title: The Impact of Sovereign Credit Ratings on Foreign Capital Inflows: Evidence from G20 Economies
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of sovereign credit ratings on Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs) and Foreign Portfolio Investments (FPIs) across G20 countries over a period of 8 years (ie. 2012 to 2019). A numerically standardized credit rating index based on ratings from the following agencies-S&P Global Ratings, Moody's, and Fitch-is analysed alongside key control variables such as GDP growth rate, inflation rate, political stability index, trade openness, exchange rate volatility and business confidence index. The study uses a panel data econometric approach using annual data of 19 G20 countries and the Euro Area. Both fixed & random effects models are estimated and the Hausman test is used to guide model selection. The findings show that stronger credit ratings significantly impact investor decisions because these ratings serve as a key metric in assessing investment risk and potential. Specifically, a one unit improvement in sovereign credit rating is associated with 8.47% increase in FDI and 6.22% increase in FPI inflows. Political stability and GDP growth are also strong positive predictors of foreign capital inflows, while trade openness shows a positive but varying degree of significance. This highlights the importance of sound macroeconomic fundamentals and institutional stability in attracting foreign capital inflows.

title: Funding Timing and No-Arbitrage Bounds in Decentralized Perpetual Markets
affiliations: and

detail.title: Funding Timing and No-Arbitrage Bounds in Decentralized Perpetual Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper

detail.abstract: This paper shows that the empirical content of no-arbitrage bounds for decentralized perpetual futures depends on whether protocol funding is known at trade entry. Building on the centralizedexchange benchmark of Dai, Li, and Yang (2025), we study two leading on-chain venues, Drift Protocol and dYdX v4, whose funding rules differ in the timing at which the arbitrageur can lock in funding income. The mechanism is general. If the next funding transfer is fixed at entry, realized funding can enter a one-period no-arbitrage bound. If funding is forward-looking, only a guaranteed floor or cap known at entry can enter the bound. Drift is the observable-funding case: its funding rate is determined from entry-time EMA-TWAP state variables, so realized funding tightens the bound even when the cap does not bind. dYdX is the forward-looking case: funding is computed from subsequent premium samples, so the argument has empirical content only in clamped regimes. Using BTC, ETH, and SOL data, we find that Drift produces informative empirical bands with out-of-band rates of 3 to 5 percent and short-lived deviations that subsequently mean revert. On dYdX, the relevant caps are so wide that they do not bind in our sample, leaving the theoretical restriction valid but empirically uninformative. Protocol funding design is therefore not a neutral implementation detail; it determines whether no-arbitrage restrictions are empirically testable.

title: Trade and Democracy in Sub-Saharan African Countries: A Sector-Based Analysis
affiliations: University of Lomé

detail.title: Trade and Democracy in Sub-Saharan African Countries: A Sector-Based Analysis
detail.abstract: The trade literature mostly considers that openness drives democracy through exogenous economic forces that exacerbate divisions between elites. However, international trade also affects the interactions between elites and citizens, which influence democracy. The Heckscher-Ohlin-Samuelson theorem predicts that countries that export labourintensive goods may see a rise in labour's reward and a reduction of the gap between the incomes of labour and capital, fostering democracy as citizens gain economic power and become a counterweight to the elites. Despite being labour abundant, Sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries are still lagging in moving towards democracy. We analyse the effect of agricultural, manufacturing and mining goods exports on democracy in SSA countries, considering elite-citizen dynamic. We rely on two-stage least squares regressions on crosssectional data, pooled two-stage least squares and system generalised method of moments estimation techniques on dynamic panel data with three different measures of democracy for robustness checks. We find no consistent significant effects of agricultural and mining exports on democracy. On the contrary, democratic institutions evolve alongside exports of manufactured goods. Trade composition, shaped by historical patterns of colonisation in developing countries, offers insights into institutions. SSA countries should develop their manufacturing sector to pave the way for solid democratic institutions.

title: Reaching for Yield Through Liquidity Risk: A Conceptual Model of Life Insurers' Appetite Across Interest-Rate Environments
affiliations: Jacksonville University (Florida) - Davis College of Business

detail.title: Reaching for Yield Through Liquidity Risk: A Conceptual Model of Life Insurers' Appetite Across Interest-Rate Environments
detail.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual model explaining how the U.S. life insurance industry's liquidity-risk appetite may evolve across interest-rate environments. Liquidity-risk posture is conceptualized as the industry's willingness to hold less liquid income producing assets, particularly mortgage loans and privately placed bonds. The model integrates reaching for yield, asset-liability management constraints, and institutional adaptation under constraint. It argues that liquidity-risk is a distinct and underexplored channel through which life insurers may pursue incremental yield when risk-free returns decline. The model generates three propositions about when liquidity-risk posture should strengthen, be moderated, or persist across interest-rate environments. It also identifies product mix changes, regulatory shifts, private credit market growth, and valuation effects as alternative structural pathways that future empirical research should evaluate.

title: Optimal Social Media Regulation

detail.title: Optimal Social Media Regulation
detail.abstract: Social media can create a collective trap: individuals may stay active on a platform not for its intrinsic value, but to avoid social exclusion and the fear of missing out (FOMO). While standard economic intuition suggests correcting this externality with a Pigovian tax, optimal regulation must also account for the platform's endogenous monetization strategy and the non-contractibility of its advertising choices. I develop a model where a monopolistic platform balances subscription pricing and ad-driven quality degradation to exploit heterogeneous consumers. I show that the platform's optimal menu has at most two items, and under a standard distributional assumption it collapses to a single posted price. My framework reveals a fundamental tension between the FOMO-driven social trap that forces over-adoption and classic monopoly pricing that drives under-adoption. I show that the optimal regulation depends on the platform's ad-monetization capability: the regulator may need to subsidize subscription-heavy platforms to offset monopoly exclusion; tax mixed-model platforms to curb ad-driven over-expansion; and impose a total ban when extreme ad-monetization destroys the platform's intrinsic value, leaving only a purely extractive collective trap.

title: Inflation and Unemployment: Different Manifestations of the Same Underlying Socioeconomic Instability Process

detail.title: Inflation and Unemployment: Different Manifestations of the Same Underlying Socioeconomic Instability Process

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE
declarations.ethicsApproval: NONE
declarations.funderStatement: NONE

detail.abstract: In macroeconomics, inflation and unemployment are usually treated as separate variables connected through frameworks such as the Phillips Curve. However, this study proposes that both are different manifestations of the same underlying socioeconomic instability process. Inflation and unemployment are not independent phenomena; rather, they are dual expressions of a single socioeconomic distortion process that simultaneously reduces purchasing power, productive stability, and human welfare. Therefore, inflation and unemployment should not be viewed as isolated macroeconomic problems, but as interconnected channels of economic leakage that continuously weaken economic growth and socioeconomic stability within society. In response to this perspective, this paper proposes a new macroeconomic indicator called Econodamage (-Ё), which integrates inflation and unemployment into a single practical index designed to evaluate the combined damage generated by both phenomena simultaneously in the formation and calculation of GDP at real prices.

title: Economic Criminology in the Digital Era: Algorithmic Detection of Money Laundering and Tax Evasion in Blockchain Networks

detail.title: Economic Criminology in the Digital Era: Algorithmic Detection of Money Laundering and Tax Evasion in Blockchain Networks
detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of blockchain-based financial systems has fundamentally transformed the structure of economic crime. While distributed ledger technologies provide unprecedented transparency, they simultaneously enable pseudonymous interactions that can be exploited for illicit financial activities, including money laundering and tax evasion. 
This paper develops a theoretical and computational framework for detecting illicit financial behavior in blockchain networks. By integrating economic criminology, graph-based analysis, and machine learning techniques, it proposes a composite detection model capable of identifying suspicious transaction patterns through structural and behavioral indicators. 
The study argues that blockchain-based financial crime is not hidden but structurally embedded within transparent systems, requiring algorithmic interpretation rather than traditional investigative approaches. The findings highlight the importance of scalable, data-driven enforcement mechanisms and coordinated regulatory responses in addressing financial crime in decentralized environments.

title: Reflections on Neo-Developmentalism in the Light of the Lula’s Governments
affiliations: and Universidade de São Paulo

detail.title: Reflections on Neo-Developmentalism in the Light of the Lula’s Governments
detail.abstract: Since the mid-2000s, the maintenance of the orthodox macroeconomic regime of the Lula's governments surprised several intellectuals in the applied social sciences sector. What marks Lula's government, especially, are two characteristics: i) the economic growth with the commodities boom or the commodities super cycle, and ii) the fight against poverty. This second phenomenon propitiated for a group of intellectuals to formulate the thesis that Brazil would be in a process of "social developmentalism". On the other hand, a fraction of economists met to formulate a new theory, the "new developmentalism", criticizing the process of de-industrialization, debt crisis and external dependence that occurred in Brazil. These two theoretical currents formed what some academics called "neo-developmentalism". This article proposes to make a critical reflection and differentiation on the two currents.

title: Institutional Environment and Cross-Border Collaborative Innovation: The Role of Trade Agreements
affiliations: School of Economics, Zhejiang University

detail.title: Institutional Environment and Cross-Border Collaborative Innovation: The Role of Trade Agreements
detail.abstract: Collaborative innovation activities are largely confined within a same country or region, which restricts firms' access to international technological frontiers and global knowledge networks. By exploiting the enforcement of regional trade agreements from 2002 to 2022 across 172 economies, I investigate how such transnational institutional arrangements shape firms' engagement in cross-border collaborative innovation. I find that the enforcement of regional trade agreements increases cross-border collaborative patents by 37.12%. Regarding the potential mechanisms, the positive effect of regional trade agreements is particularly pronounced for country pairs with initially large regulatory differences, suggesting that institutional convergence can lower the compliance costs associated with cross-border collaboration. In addition, the effect is concentrated in industries that are sensitive to intellectual property rights, indicating that improvements in institutional frameworks, especially stronger intellectual property protection, reduce firms' perceived risks and costs of knowledge leakage.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a state-conditioned local adjustment framework to analyze how aggregate demand components interact when aggregate income follows a given trajectory. Departing from conventional income-adjusting and equilibrium-correction approaches, the framework distinguishes between income states and local deviations, and examines where adjustment is absorbed when income does not freely respond. The analysis introduces two diagnostic tests: a consumption buffering test and a fiscal absorption test. These tests do not estimate marginal effects or causal relationships. Instead, they assess whether local deviations among demand components are absorbed through internal reallocation or accommodated through income expansion. Applying the framework to aggregate data, the paper finds no evidence of local adjustment through either consumption or taxation. Both tests indicate an expansion-accommodating regime, in which aggregate income absorbs deviations rather than forcing reallocation among demand components. This result clarifies why standard interpretations based on crowding-out or marginal effects may be misleading. By shifting the focus from effect estimation to state diagnosis, the paper contributes a measurement framework for identifying how economies adjust under different income regimes. The approach integrates insights from Keynesian, post-Keynesian, and stockflow consistent traditions, while providing a clear empirical diagnostic for political economy analysis.
