title: Structural Market Microstructure: Energy Absorption and Limit-Point Bifurcation in the LQD Market, January-March 2020

detail.title: Structural Market Microstructure: Energy Absorption and Limit-Point Bifurcation in the LQD Market, January-March 2020
detail.abstract: This study identifies a 13-trading-day lead indicator for the March 2020 liquidity collapse in the LQD corporate bond ETF market. Using intraday top-of-book data from Databento (XNYS.PILLAR, tbbo schema, January-March 2020), we document that spread volatility inflects upward on February 24, 2020, while the median spread remains pinned at the $0.01 tick floor, presaging the catastrophic spread expansion of March 9 by 13 trading days. We interpret this pattern through the lens of bistable structural mechanics: the market enters a metastable loading phase in which dealer intermediation clamps the observable price structure while the system absorbs internal energy, culminating in a limit-point bifurcation. The volatility inflection is a "structural warming" signal, invisible to conventional spread-level monitoring. A Chow structural break scan (F = 17.4, p < 0.001) confirms a discrete change in the spread-generating process on March 1, between the volatility inflection and the visible collapse. We argue that top-of-book (TBBO) data are sufficient to identify this precursor but insufficient to measure critical slowing down in the autocorrelation structure, which requires limit-order-book depth (L2) data. This paper is a companion to Yun (2026a), which documents the macro-level ratchet migration of price discovery in investment-grade corporate credit from dealer-polled benchmarks to LQD over 2013-2020.

title: Path Integral Formulation of Option Pricing Beyond Black-Scholes: A Unified Framework for Jump-Diffusion and Rough Volatility
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Path Integral Formulation of Option Pricing Beyond Black-Scholes: A Unified Framework for Jump-Diffusion and Rough Volatility
detail.abstract: The Black-Scholes framework, while analytically tractable, rests on two empirically untenable assumptions: that price returns are Gaussian, and that volatility is a deterministic constant. Decades of high-frequency data contradict both. This paper develops a unified path integral formulation of European option pricing that accommodates(i) jump-diffusion processes(Lévy noise), and(ii) rough stochastic volatility driven by fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H ≈ 0.1. We begin from first principles, establishing the correspondence between the Feynman path integral and the risk-neutral pricing kernel, and show how the Black-Scholes result emerges as the Gaussian saddle-point approximation of a more general functional integral. We then extend the Lagrangian of the system to incorporate power-law jump kernels and a fractional noise action. Under the rough volatility extension, the non-Markovian nature of fractional Brownian motion is treated via a Volterra-type action functional. We derive semi-analytical approximations to the transition probability density and the resulting implied volatility surface, demonstrating that the path integral framework naturally reproduces the empirically observed power-law ATM skew decay ∂σ impl /∂k ∼ T H-1/2 without fitting. The framework provides a principled physicsbased derivation of phenomena currently handled by calibrated, empirically-motivated models(rough Bergomi, SABR), and opens avenues for perturbative corrections via Feynman diagram techniques imported directly from quantum field theory.

title: Reforms to Stimulate Business Investment in Greece: Assessing the Impact of  Judicial Efficiency, Governance Quality and Tax Wedge Reduction
affiliations: Alpha Bank, Chief Economist, Alpha Bank, University of Pireaus and Bank of Greece

detail.title: Reforms to Stimulate Business Investment in Greece: Assessing the Impact of  Judicial Efficiency, Governance Quality and Tax Wedge Reduction
detail.abstract:
The long-lasting recession following the 2009 sovereign crisis in Greece left a harmful legacy, causing considerable impairments to capital stock. Disinvestment grew and fixed capital depreciation remained higher than fixed capital formation for a prolonged period, from 2010 to 2021, resulting in erosion of capital stock and the creation of an investment gap. At the same time, prolonged disinvestment posed obstacles to the uptake of new technologies, leading to productivity losses, as labour was combined with capital of lower quality. The investment gap defined as the "erosion" of the country's natural capital stock during the period when  depreciation exceeded fresh investment was quite significant and measured close to €95 bn at current prices. 
This paper examines the potential impact of three specific areas of reforms, which are either in a process of implementation but subject to delay or in the phase of designing. These reforms consist of an improvement in judicial efficiency the quality of governance and the further reduction of the labour tax wedge for employers and employees. The reason why we focus on these three areas is that they are major building blocks of the business environment of a country because they determine the main parameters considered by domestic or foreign investors before proceeding with the implementation of a new investment project (e.g., operational costs and in particular cost of labour, regulatory barriers and rules and the institutional framework). Therefore, the implementation of these three building blocks of reforms is expected not only to speed up domestic and foreign investment, with multiplying positive effects on the formation of new capital stock and the closing of the income gap with EU economies, but also to pave the way for sustainable growth over a long-term horizon.

title: Designing and Implementing an Organizational Cybersecurity Governance Training Program Based on the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: A Practitioner Curriculum Model

detail.title: Designing and Implementing an Organizational Cybersecurity Governance Training Program Based on the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: A Practitioner Curriculum Model
detail.abstract: The National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework version 2.0 (NIST CSF 2.0), released in February 2024, represents the most significant revision to the framework since its original publication in 2014. A central feature of this revision is the formal elevation of Governance (GV) to a standalone, cross-cutting function-signaling a shift in industry expectations toward treating cybersecurity as an enterprise risk discipline rather than a purely technical domain. This working paper presents an original, practitioner-designed training curriculum comprising 26 structured sessions organized across eight thematic modules. The curriculum is designed to operationalize NIST CSF 2.0 at the organizational level through a train-the-trainer model, enabling internal practitioners to build durable cybersecurity governance competencies across functional roles-from executive leadership to operational personnel. The paper documents the curriculum architecture, instructional design rationale, learning objective framework, facilitation methodology, and assessment model. It positions cybersecurity governance training not as compliance overhead, but as a strategic organizational capability. The curriculum is designed to be institution-agnostic and applicable across government, regulated industries, healthcare, financial services, and higher education environments. This paper establishes the original authorship, design framework, and intellectual property of the curriculum as developed independently by the author. The model presented herein has not been derived from, commissioned by, or produced in any institutional capacity.

title: Three Frameworks, One Worker? The demographic gradient of automation risk in Latin America

detail.abstract: Latin American economies are entering the Fourth Industrial Revolution with high informality, persistent gender, education, and age inequalities, and limited institutional buffering against technological displacement. Whether automation amplifies those inequalities depends on whether the workers most exposed are also those already disadvantaged. We test this by integrating the three leading automation-risk frameworks-Frey and Osborne (2017), Autor, Levy, and Murnane (2003), and Webb (2020)-as three independent measurements of a latent worker-level exposure, estimated jointly through a generalised linear model with an expectation-maximisation algorithm (Ibrahim, 1990). Using harmonised worker-level microdata from the World Bank's STEP and OECD's PIAAC surveys for seven Latin American economies (Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Mexico, Peru) and an OECD comparison group, we recover the joint skilltask-demographic structure of automation risk under all three frameworks simultaneously. Four findings emerge. First, average automation risk in Latin America ranges from 0.54 in Bolivia (the same as the OECD average) to 0.65 in El Salvador, with the regional premium driven primarily by El Salvador, Mexico, Peru, and Colombia. Second, the education and age gradients converge across all three frameworks: less-educated and younger workers face elevated exposure under Frey-Osborne, Autor, and Webb simultaneously. title: Conditional Skill Compression: Domain Expertise and the Unequal Returns to Generative AI

detail.title: Conditional Skill Compression: Domain Expertise and the Unequal Returns to Generative AI
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence creates a distributional paradox: AI compresses withinoccupation productivity gaps, yet aggregate inequality is not falling. This paper resolves the paradox through a formal model built around two thresholds. The Minimum Expertise Threshold (θ*) is the minimum domain knowledge required to evaluate and correct AI outputs safely; it is derived endogenously from expected AI-use payoffs. The model yields three predictions. First, the within-occupation gap between qualified and high-skill workers narrows, as medium-skill workers above the threshold fill their execution gap through AI while high-skill workers approach the productivity ceiling. Second, the gap between qualified and below-threshold workers widens, as below-threshold workers gain little by AI they cannot evaluate. Third, AI adoption also reduces demand for entry-level workers who would otherwise accumulate the domain knowledge (θ*) needed to cross the threshold, generating a training-pipeline externality: total discounted welfare can fall even when the static productivity gain is positive.

title: Bank Sectoral Concentration and Carbon-Intensive Lending
affiliations: Monash Business School - Department of Banking and Finance,  and Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance

detail.title: Bank Sectoral Concentration and Carbon-Intensive Lending
detail.abstract: This paper examines how banks' sectoral concentration affects lending to carbon-intensive firms following the Paris Agreement. Using two decades of international syndicated-loan data, we show that banks with prior market presence in a borrower's industry continue to supply credit to carbon-intensive firms after 2015, whereas entrant banks reduce lending. Firms borrowing from experienced banks obtain larger loans, increase leverage and asset growth, and hold more cash, while subsequently reducing emissions over longer horizons. The results highlight the importance of banks' preexisting industry positions in shaping climate-related credit allocation and corporate transition outcomes.

title: Beyond Rational Economic Man: A Three-Layer Model of Muslim Consumer Decision-Making Grounded in Maqasid al-Shariah and Khaldunian Social Theory

detail.title: Beyond Rational Economic Man: A Three-Layer Model of Muslim Consumer Decision-Making Grounded in Maqasid al-Shariah and Khaldunian Social Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable as this study uses publicly available financial and market data and does not involve human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract:
Mainstream economic theory models consumer behaviour through the lens of Rational Economic Man (REM) — an autonomous agent who maximises utility through price and quality comparisons. This paper challenges the universal applicability of the REM model in Muslim-majority markets by developing a Three-Layer Model of Muslim Consumer DecisionMaking, theoretically grounded in the Maqasid al-Shariah framework and Khaldunian social theory. The model disaggregates consumer motivation into three analytically distinct layers: (1) maslaha-based rational-economic considerations, (2) hifz al-din — the religious and ethical compliance layer, and (3) 'asabiyyah — collective identity and geopolitical solidarity.
The paper tests this theoretical framework against the empirical case of Americana Restaurants International PLC, which recorded a 40% profit decline and a 47% stock price fall in 2024 following consumer boycotts in its MENA markets. The evidence demonstrates that the 2024 demand collapse was not explicable within a REM framework but is fully predictable within the Three-Layer Model: a Layer Three ('asabiyyah) activation event overrode all Layer One price-utility calculations, rendering conventional marketing responses ineffective. The paper further integrates analysis of government interventions — including Saudi Arabia's VAT increase and Nitaqat localisation policy — within an Islamic political economy lens.
The Three-Layer Model is advanced as a generalizable framework applicable to any market in which identity, collective obligation, or religious values constitute significant dimensions of consumer choice. The paper concludes with strategic and policy recommendations grounded in Islamic economic principles, and with an agenda for future empirical research to quantitatively test the model's propositions.

title: Motivation Without Hierarchy: Symbolic-Functional Dynamics as a New Conceptual Architecture
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Motivation Without Hierarchy: Symbolic-Functional Dynamics as a New Conceptual Architecture
detail.abstract:
Hierarchical models have long dominated the theoretical study of human motivation (Maslow, 1943; Alderfer, 1969), portraying motivational organization as a sequential progression governed by the ordered satisfaction of discrete needs. Despite their conceptual clarity, these models rely on an underexamined assumption: that motivational structure is inherently hierarchical. This article challenges this assumption by identifying a fundamental limitation in prevailing theories—the absence of a framework capable of accounting for the simultaneous operation of symbolic meaning and functional constraints within a unified system.

In response, the article develops a non-hierarchical, process-based framework in which motivation is conceptualized as a dynamic evaluative configuration emerging from the continuous interaction between two interdependent dimensions: the symbolic and the functional. The symbolic dimension encompasses meaning, identity, and recognition, whereas the functional dimension concerns effectiveness, constraint management, and outcome realization. These dimensions operate concurrently within a single evaluative structure, where behavioral selection is determined by the relative weighting of symbolic value, functional return, and their associated constraints under context-sensitive conditions.

Within this framework, motivational stability and tension are not attributed to simple alignment or misalignment between dimensions. Instead, they arise from differences in net evaluative value across competing alternatives, shaped by constraint pressures and contextual weighting. Stability emerges when one alternative achieves a clear evaluative dominance, whereas fluctuation arises when values converge or when constraints impede decisional resolution.

This framework provides a unified explanation for phenomena that remain difficult to account for within hierarchical models, including persistence under deprivation, commitment without functional return, and meaning-driven collective action. As a conceptual contribution, it establishes a foundation for future work aimed at formalization, empirical operationalization, and integration with neurocognitive models of evaluative processing.

title: Beyond LCOE: Methodological Limitations and a Macroeconomic Framework for Energy Transition Costs
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast

detail.title: Beyond LCOE: Methodological Limitations and a Macroeconomic Framework for Energy Transition Costs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest to declare.

detail.abstract: While Levelised Cost of Electricity (LCOE) can be useful as a project-level screening tool, it is not a reliable basis for comparing electricity generation technologies or assessing the wider cost of energy transition. Standard LCOE calculations embed inconsistent discount rates, overlook end-use differences, omit key technologies such as nuclear from headline comparisons, and treat projected carbon prices as fixed inputs rather than uncertain policy variables. Individually and in combination, these methodological choices distort cost comparisons and risk misleading policy decisions. To address this, the report introduces a simple macroeconomic framework that links persistent changes in the real cost of energy to national income using a small number of observable variables, making the cost of transition explicit and testable under alternative scenarios. Together, these insights highlight the need to move beyond narrow generation metrics toward more transparent, economy-wide assessments of energy transition costs.

title: Does Openness Amplify Money-Financed Fiscal Stimulus? A Fiscal Theory Perspective
affiliations: Nagoya City University and Chuo University

detail.title: Does Openness Amplify Money-Financed Fiscal Stimulus? A Fiscal Theory Perspective
detail.abstract: Does economic openness enhance or diminish the effectiveness of money-financed (MF) fiscal stimulus? This study reexamines this question within a small open economy framework, emphasizing the fiscal regime governing government debt valuation. While Okano and Eguchi (2024), building on Galí (2020), show that MF fiscal expansions generate larger output responses as openness increases, we demonstrate that this conclusion is not robust when the fiscal theory of the price level (FTPL) is operative. Under the FTPL, the relationship between openness and the output response to MF fiscal stimulus becomes fiscal-regime contingent. Specifically, under normal conditions, greater openness weakens the output response, reversing the positive openness-multiplier relationship documented in the existing literature. In contrast, under strong deflationary pressure such as at the zero lower bound, greater openness amplifies the output response, although through a distinct transmission mechanism. Our analysis is primarily a positive, regime-comparison study. As a supplementary normative benchmark, we also report a welfare comparison based on a second-order approximation of household utility. The broader implication is cautionary: policy conclusions drawn under a Ricardian framework may not generalize to environments in which fiscal-monetary interactions are central to price-level determination.

title: Basic Sanitation and Environmental Health in Vulnerable Urban Contexts: Empirical Evidence From Sullana, Peru
affiliations: UNIVERSIDAD CESAR VALLEJO S.A.C.

detail.title: Basic Sanitation and Environmental Health in Vulnerable Urban Contexts: Empirical Evidence From Sullana, Peru
detail.abstract: The study analyzes the relationship between basic sanitation and environmental impact in households in a popular urbanization of Sullana during the year 2025, using a quantitative, non-experimental and correlational approach applied to 305 households through a questionnaire validated by experts and with a reliability of α = 0.803. The variables evaluated were basic sanitation (access to services, wastewater management, and solid waste management) and environmental impact, measured through environmental health, disease risk, and vector control indicators. The results show that basic sanitation is at a regular level in most households (66.89%), while environmental health is deficient in more than 50% of homes. Pearson's correlations show positive and significant relationships between basic sanitation and environmental health (r = .307), disease risk (r = .310), vector control (r = .454), and overall environmental impact (r = .464), indicating that better sanitation conditions reduce health and environmental vulnerability. However, structural factors such as health education, domestic practices, and institutional constraints moderate these effects. The study concludes that strengthening sanitation infrastructure, improving waste management and promoting sustainable practices is essential to reduce environmental and health risks, contributing to the fulfillment of Sustainable Development Goals 6 and 11. This work provides localized evidence that can guide public policies and community programs in vulnerable urban contexts.

title: Stability of Repeated Decision Systems: A Dynamical Model of Institutional Exposure and Participation

detail.title: Stability of Repeated Decision Systems: A Dynamical Model of Institutional Exposure and Participation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects, identifiable personal data, or clinical intervention. The analysis is based on theoretical modeling, computational simulation, synthetic administrative processes, and publicly available policy information; therefore, institutional review board approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Public benefit participation is often modeled as a static function of eligibility and compliance, yet many exits arise through repeated administrative interaction rather than changes in underlying eligibility. We develop a dynamic exposure-based framework in which administrative interactions generate a latent exposure stock that accumulates over time and modifies transition risks between participation, procedural failure, and system exit. Exposure evolves through a load-recovery process governed by the balance between interaction-driven inflow and institutional recovery capacity. Within this framework, participation dynamics depend not only on eligibility conditions, but on the stability of the underlying interaction process. Exposure-dependent transitions generate nonlinear concentration of exit risk in the upper tail of the exposure distribution, producing a dispersion-fragility mechanism in which persistence amplifies concentrated failure and disenrollment. The analysis identifies a duration-absorption tradeoff in which higher administrative intensity can simultaneously increase exit rates while reducing measured average exposure by accelerating absorption into disenrollment states. As a result, conventional burden metrics may systematically understate instability in high-intensity administrative regimes. Computational experiments characterize regime behavior under variation in exposure intensity, recovery capacity, persistence, and procedural failure dynamics. The results show that instability emerges gradually through exposure accumulation and propagates through delayed transition responses rather than through immediate collapse. More broadly, the framework characterizes a class of repeated-interaction systems in which cumulative burden, recovery dynamics, and absorbing exit states jointly govern participation stability.

title: Trade-Dress Law in India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad and Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

detail.title: Trade-Dress Law in India
detail.abstract: The increased emphasis on visual presentation and brand experience has elevated trade-dress from a peripheral concern to a central feature of trademark protection. Indian trade-dress protection is currently spread across multiple intellectual property legal regime with special emphasis through the passing-off law under the trademarks Act 1999. Despite commercial importance of trade-dress law, and without explicit statutory definition of what constitutes trade-dress, its protection is shaped almost entirely through a patchwork of judicial interpretation across the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The present study undertakes a mapping and comparative analysis of trade-dress jurisprudence across the Supreme Court of India and four major High Courts; Delhi, Bombay, Madras and Calcutta. The analysis reveals a fragmented landscape highlighting divergent judicial approaches to distinctiveness, consumer perception, functionality, and evidentiary thresholds. The present study further identifies persistent doctrinal tensions from the conflation of trade-dress with copyright and design law in the Indian context. The authors argue for a more disciplined and coherent framework for trade-dress protection in India.

title: The Anticipatory Real Effects of Accounting Standard Change: The Case of the Current Expected Credit Loss Adoption
affiliations: Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business - Rice University, Southern Methodist University (SMU) - SMU Cox School of Business and Rice University

detail.title: The Anticipatory Real Effects of Accounting Standard Change: The Case of the Current Expected Credit Loss Adoption
detail.abstract: The Current Expected Credit Loss (CECL) model forced banks to build more forward-looking credit-risk systems well before formal adoption. Exploiting the 2016-2020 preparation window, we examine whether these mandated informational upgrades altered lending decisions even while the incurred loss model remained in force. Such real effects represent an unintended externality of the standard-setting process and speak directly to a core evaluation criterion in the FASB's post-implementation review (PIR) framework. Using an affectedness-based design, we compare banks with relatively low reserve coverage at the onset of the transition to otherwise similar banks, after entropy balancing on observable lending and risk characteristics. We find that low-reserve banks, especially those with riskier portfolios, reduce lending growth but increase portfolio risk and loan profitability relative to comparable banks. These patterns suggest that CECL-induced improvements in information systems enhanced screening and credit-risk assessment, leading to more efficient lending decisions before the standard took effect. More broadly, our evidence highlights an important anticipatory real effect of accounting standard changes that operates through information production rather than through the mechanical effects of financial reporting.

title: From Productive Catch-Up to Technological Parity: Dating the Sequential Catch-Up of Chinese Photovoltaics, 2000–2023
affiliations: Domaine Universitaire

detail.title: From Productive Catch-Up to Technological Parity: Dating the Sequential Catch-Up of Chinese Photovoltaics, 2000–2023
detail.abstract: European photovoltaic re-shoring policies rest on the assumption that EU dependence on China is industrial rather than technological. We reassess China's technological trajectory in photovoltaics over 2000-2023 using 370,462 INPADOC patent families extracted from Google Patents Public Data (CPC scope Y02E10/5*). Each family is represented as a share vector in a 378-dimension technical space, aggregated at country-year and firm-year levels. Three measures are computed: cosine between technology profiles (Jaffe approach), the patent quality indicators of Kelly et al. (2021) transformed into annual ranks, and endogenous breakpoint detection via PELT. Results reveal a two-phase sequential chronology. A first statistical break in 2006 marks the convergence of the Chinese technology profile toward the basket of historical leaders (Japan, United States, Germany, Korea), with mean cosine rising from 0.42 to 0.74 over the period. A shift in the quality hierarchy follows between 2010 and 2014: China's mean Q-index rank improves from 3.25 to 1.20 across five countries, while Germany moves in the opposite direction. The 4-to-8-year lag between the two transitions is consistent with an imitation-then-innovation process and does not match the predictions of competing scenarios. A third result nuances this picture: aggregate convergence is carried by the long tail of the Chinese ecosystem (universities, start-ups, peripheral actors), not by leader firms, which oscillate around stable positions in the technology space without net directional drift. Within the international subcorpus, the long tail also dominates the eight Chinese industrial leaders on the Kelly Q-index (median 1.005 vs 0.518, p < 0.001), confirming that distributed innovation operates on quality as well as on positional dynamics. These findings indicate that European dependence on Chinese photovoltaics is now technological as well as industrial, which challenges the founding premise of current re-shoring policies.

title: Counterfactuals and Causal Identification in Legal Damages

detail.title: Counterfactuals and Causal Identification in Legal Damages
detail.abstract: The but-for question, what would have happened absent the defendant's wrong? sits at the center of compensatory damages across every legal system. This paper argues that damages practice has a problem with that question not at the level of estimation, where most of the debate is focused, but at the prior levels of defining the counterfactual and establishing whether it can be recovered from available evidence. Drawing on the econometric causal framework of Heckman and Pinto (2023), the paper shows that damages analysis requires three tasks kept separated defining the counterfactual as a thought experiment, establishing whether it is identified from available data, and only then estimating it, and that the collapse of these tasks into a single exercise produces damages figures that are less reliable than they appear, regardless of the sophistication of the estimation technique. A further distinction is developed between parametric uncertainty, which standard valuation methods are designed to reflect, and structural indeterminacy, which renders the expectation underlying any forward-looking valuation undefined. DCF analysis, the dominant method in investment arbitration, is suited to the former and may become unreliable when applied to the latter. These arguments are developed through eight significant arbitral awards, diagnosing the causal inference failure in each. The same failures are shown to appear in antitrust and patent damages contexts. A three-step protocol, define, identify, estimate, is proposed that damages experts and adjudicators can apply without specialized econometric training.

title: Insurance-Based Disparities in Home Health Care Utilization and Spending: Evidence from a Three-Part Model
affiliations: and School of Economic, Political and Policy Sciences

detail.title: Insurance-Based Disparities in Home Health Care Utilization and Spending: Evidence from a Three-Part Model
detail.abstract: This study examines insurance-based disparities in home health care (HHC) utilization and expenditures in the United States using a three-part hurdle model applied to pooled Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data from 2006 to 2023. We decompose the spending process into three distinct margins: the probability of access (Hurdle 1), the likelihood that use results in a billable episode (Hurdle 2), and spending intensity conditional on payment (Hurdle 3). Our findings reveal that disparities are primarily driven by upstream access and "billability" margins rather than downstream treatment intensity. While fee-for-service (FFS) Medicare and Medicare Advantage (MA) exhibit nearly identical access rates (approximately 3 percent), MA beneficiaries incur roughly 20 percent lower expected expenditures per user ($1,281 vs. $1,602), suggesting that managed care constraints operate through episode-level management rather than gatekeeping at the point of entry. Furthermore, HHC is characterized by payer-specific billing disparities-with probabilities ranging from 0.70 for private insurance to 0.88 for Medicaidthat are absent in a placebo analysis of outpatient care, where billing is standardized at over 95 percent across all insurers. Finally, we find that Medicaid accounts for the highest populationlevel spending, exceeding $337 per adult, reflecting an institutional pipeline in which health shocks and the exhaustion of assets ("spend-down") trigger enrollment. Overall, the results suggest that HHC spending patterns are shaped by institutional coverage design and a safety-net structure where financial ruin often precedes public assistance.

title: One Wall Away: Campus Closures, Visitor Access, and the Micro-Geography of Innovation
affiliations: , The University of Seoul, Singapore Management University and Institute of Urban Development, Nanjing Audit University

detail.title: One Wall Away: Campus Closures, Visitor Access, and the Micro-Geography of Innovation
detail.abstract: How much does local innovation depend on outsiders' in-person presence on university campuses? We exploit the nationwide closure of walled Chinese university campuses triggered by COVID-19, which sustained a block on outsider access well beyond the pandemic. We find that patenting in the innermost ring (0-2 km) fell by 5.8% relative to that in the outermost ring (8-10 km), with the magnitude decaying with distance. Both spillover and coordination-platform mechanisms likely operate: collaborative patents fell, including those without university inventors, while solo patents rose. Anonymized mobility data show that campus visits collapsed in the same pattern, accounting for a large share of the patent decline. Restricting in-person access to a university imposes substantial innovation costs on the surrounding economy.

title: Structural Decoupling in Equity Markets: A Spectral Heterogeneity Index for Resilient Portfolio Diversification
affiliations: CAEN - UFC

detail.title: Structural Decoupling in Equity Markets: A Spectral Heterogeneity Index for Resilient Portfolio Diversification
detail.abstract: Portfolio diversification presupposes that assets exhibiting low correlation during normal periods retain that property under stress-a premise that the empirical evidence systematically contradicts. This paper proposes the Spectral Heterogeneity Index (SHI), a scalar measure of the relative deviation between the oscillation frequency of an individual asset's medium-term price cycle and the market average frequency, extracted via the Baxter-King filter and the Hilbert transform with an analytic guarantee of the Bedrosian condition. Applied to 316 S&P 500 constituents over the period 2007-2026, the SHI identifies 8 assets with significant spectral heterogeneity, whose crisisperiod correlation increase with the market index is 8.5 percentage points against 17 points for typical assets (Mann-Whitney p = 0.025). Subperiod analysis reveals two types of decoupling-static and dynamic-the latter being systematically understated by full-period estimates. A top-5% SHIfiltered portfolio strategy produces a Sharpe ratio of 1.195, superior to both the equal-weight benchmark (1.013) and the minimum-variance portfolio (1.174). The SHI offers a pre-crisis pre-selection criterion, computable during calm periods, that complements conventional portfolio optimization tools.

title: Quantitative Methods and Asset Pricing of Judicial Claims in Brazil: An Institutional Framework for Precatórios Funds Under the EC 136 ⁄ 2025 Regime
affiliations: Atlantis University

detail.title: Quantitative Methods and Asset Pricing of Judicial Claims in Brazil: An Institutional Framework for Precatórios Funds Under the EC 136 ⁄ 2025 Regime
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive institutional and quantitative framework for the valuation, risk management, and structuring of Brazilian judicial claims, specifically precatórios-government debt arising from final court judgments. As the secondary market for these illiquid assets matures, institutional investors and specialized funds, such as Droom Investimentos founded by Eduardo Gouvêa, have increasingly deployed advanced quantitative methods to price sovereign and subsovereign risk, legal uncertainty, and liquidity premiums embedded in these instruments. Crucially, this paper incorporates an in-depth analysis of the Constitutional Amendment (EC) 136 ⁄ 2025 , promulgated on September 9, 2025, detailing its profound impact on monetary correction (IPCA + 2% p.a., capped by the Selic rate), the staggered Net Current Revenue (RCL) payment limits (1% to 5%), the elimination of the December 31, 2029 payment deadline, and the new February 1st budgetary submission deadline. We further analyze the Provimento CNJ 207 ⁄ 2025 , which operationalized the transition rules, and explicitly model the legislative and constitutional risk introduced by the Direct Action of Unconstitutionality (ADI 7873), filed by the OAB before the STF, treating it as a distinct fifth component of risk spread with embedded upside optionality. Drawing on models including Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) with probability-weighted scenario analysis, Monte Carlo simulations using the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (Vasicek) process for stochastic interest rates, and structural credit risk frameworks, this paper bridges the gap between traditional asset pricing theory and the idiosyncratic nature of Brazilian distressed sovereign debt. A practical valuation case study is provided using market data from May 2026 (Selic 14.75%, NTN-B 5Y real 7.50%, IPCA 6.50%, CDS 180bps), alongside a 4-dimensional stress testing framework and a recalibrated internal ratings system. The paper concludes with a discussion of offshore structuring strategies to attract global institutional capital to this underexplored Brazilian alternative asset class.

title: When Do Regime Signals Work? HMM Uncertainty and Trade Execution Across Asset Classes

detail.title: When Do Regime Signals Work? HMM Uncertainty and Trade Execution Across Asset Classes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently, without any financial or commercial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects. Therefore, ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: HMM-based confidence scores are natural candidates for filtering regime-aware trade execution, yet their empirical predictive validity has not been tested across real assets and evaluation horizons. We conduct the first systematic cross-asset study of three HMM uncertainty signals, composite confidence, raw posterior entropy, and regime persistence, across eight asset classes at daily, 3-day, 5-day, 10-day, and 21-day horizons. At daily resolution, signals are largely uninformative: no individual asset achieves a significant, correctly-signed result that survives Bonferroni correction across 24 per-asset tests (α Bonferroni ≈ 0.002). Signals emerge clearly at 3-day aggregation and strengthen with horizon, with raw entropy achieving Spearman ρ =-0.411 (p < 0.001, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.555,-0.347]) for IWM at 10 days. The temporal threshold broadly aligns with empirical mean regime durations, though the relationship is not strictly linear across assets. Raw entropy outperforms composite confidence for equity indices; stay probability better predicts execution edge for cryptocurrency assets. All results use in-sample HMM fitting; reported effect sizes should be treated as upper bounds on out-of-sample predictive power. Results have direct implications for uncertainty metric design in regime-aware execution systems.

title: Donor-Side Fiscal Aging and Foreign Aid: Evidence from a 22-Country Panel and Bilateral Gravity

detail.title: Donor-Side Fiscal Aging and Foreign Aid: Evidence from a 22-Country Panel and Bilateral Gravity
detail.abstract: Dupas, Goldberg, and Pande (2026) characterise the 2025 collapse in official development assistance (ODA) as a response to donor fiscal pressure, leaving the underlying mechanism unspecified. This paper tests whether that pressure is demographic-fiscal in origin, and whether it operates as a structural amplification of aid cuts in the most aged donors or as a uniform level effect on aggregate ODA. Using a balanced 22-country panel of OECD-DAC donors over 1990-2024, a synthetic control study of the 2021 United Kingdom 0.7-to-0.5 percent of GNI cut, an event study of the 1995 Canadian Chrétien-Martin budget, a triple-difference within the eurozone austerity cohort, and a 1995-2024 bilateral gravity panel of 22 donors and 190 recipients, I find that aged donors give less in aggregate but the cut does not amplify with aging on any of six independent margins: a decade-split panel, a level spline at one standard deviation above the mean of the demographic index, a within-cohort triple-difference at high old-age dependency, the donor-recipient demographic gap in bilateral gravity, geographic distance, and allocation concentration. The donor-side fiscal-aging channel is best characterised as uniform compression of total ODA, not as cascade-zone amplification or recipient-reshaping. The basic slope survives at borderline significance (p ≈ 0.06-0.10) and is heavily levered on the United Kingdom; the 2025 U.S. outturn-a 57 percent real cut-sits within the panel-implied 95 percent prediction interval but in the lower tail. The narrowing is the contribution: the paper makes the demographic mechanism behind the headline 2025 ODA decline explicit while rejecting the demographic-amplification framings a less-tested mechanism-explicit reading would have endorsed.

title: Measuring Editorial Noise: A Retrospective Suppression Index for Public Broadcasting Content Analysis
affiliations: (Swiss Association for Non-Biased Reporting) (SVFAB)

detail.title: Measuring Editorial Noise: A Retrospective Suppression Index for Public Broadcasting Content Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None. Self-motivated.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract: We propose a quantitative method for detecting editorial noise and suppression in public broadcasting. The Suppression Index S compares standardized changes in external outcome indicators (e.g., interest rates, consumer prices, accident statistics) with the standardized airtime share devoted to corresponding topics in broadcast transcripts. Positive S values indicate suppression (significant real-world developments receiving disproportionately low coverage), while negative values indicate noise (intensive coverage without proportional real-world change). We apply the method to a corpus of over 19,000 broadcasts from Swiss public television (SRF) across four program formats and nine thematic clusters over the period 2018-2026. Of 2,824 month×broadcaster×cluster observations, 10.3% exhibit extreme deviations (|S| > 2.0). The most pronounced noise event (S =-9.46) occurred during the Credit Suisse crisis in February 2023, when all four programs massively overemphasized interest rate coverage relative to actual monetary policy changes. The strongest suppression (S = +3.75) occurred in April 2020, when pandemic coverage displaced reporting on significant banking sector developments. Pearson correlations between outcome changes and airtime shares range from r = 0.51 (energy prices, p < 0.001) to r = 0.01 (interest rates, n.s.), revealing substantial variation in editorial proportionality across topic domains. The method is language-agnostic, reproducible, and transferable to any broadcaster with transcript data.

title:
The Gold-Silver Ratio and Dollar Hegemony:
A Systemic Geopolitical Analysis of the United States as a Gold-Centered Actor

detail.title:
The Gold-Silver Ratio and Dollar Hegemony:
A Systemic Geopolitical Analysis of the United States as a Gold-Centered Actor
detail.abstract: This article examines the gold-to-silver ratio (Au/Ag) as a market-institutional variable within the hierarchy of contemporary international monetary power. Shifting analytical focus from the silver-producing subsystem to the gold-centered hegemonic actor, it uses the methodological lens of Systemic Geopolitical Analysis (SGA) to argue that the persistently elevated Au/Ag ratio should not be understood merely as a neutral price relation between two commodities, but also as an indicator of the historical demonetization of silver and the consolidation of a gold-centered reserve order. In this order, the United States retains a privileged systemic position through the interaction of three factors: the world's largest official gold holdings, the dollar's continuing role as the leading reserve and transaction currency, and the depth of U.S. financial and institutional networks. The article traces the formation of this order from nineteenth-century silver demonetization to Bretton Woods and the post-1971 dollar system, and uses the SGA framework to explore how alternative Au/Ag regimes could affect the strategic options of dollar challengers. The central claim is not that the Au/Ag ratio alone causes dollar hegemony, but that high-ratio conditions reinforce a monetary hierarchy in which silver-centered or bimetallic alternatives face significant structural, institutional, and liquidity constraints.

title: How Do Rising Temperatures Affect Inflation Expectations?
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research, , European Central Bank (ECB) and De Nederlandsche Bank

detail.title: How Do Rising Temperatures Affect Inflation Expectations?
detail.abstract: Global temperatures are rising rapidly, yet little is known about how consumers associate climate change with expectations about the macroeconomy. We address this gap by conducting a series of experiments within a large-scale, population-representative survey of euro area consumers. A 0.5°C rise scenario in global temperatures increases five-year-ahead inflation expectations by 0.65 percentage points. Effects are stronger among consumers with greater awareness of climate change. Additionally, consumers expect adverse effects of global warming on economic growth, employment, and tax burden. Many consumers demonstrate limited willingness to pay for mitigating further temperature increases. Instead, they place primary responsibility for climate action on governments.

title: LECF -Longitudinal Emotional Concern Framework
affiliations: AIShell Labs LLC

detail.title: LECF -Longitudinal Emotional Concern Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: "The author is the founder of AIShell Labs LLC and developer of MyFriendTheAI, the reference implementation described in this paper."

detail.abstract:
In order to derive from our experiences of human and AI interaction a state of wellbeing and balance, we must acknowledge the need for a system of personal, emotional and mental safety. An LLM does not inherently differentiate between harmful and harmless content. Prompting alone, being only suggestive, is insufficient as a safeguard. We must therefore apply deterministic methodology. Yet the state of such methodology is today primitive and immature. Herein I discuss an evolutionary step in the process of realising both a physical and emotional safety protocol for human and AI interaction.
Current AI safety systems operate on a single-instance model — each input is evaluated independently for explicit harmful content. This paper argues that single-instance classification is structurally insufficient for detecting the most dangerous failure mode in consumer AI: the gradual formation of emotional dependency and the slow deterioration of user wellbeing across sessions.
I propose a Longitudinal Emotional Concern Framework (LECF) consisting of three components: a co-modifier weighted semantic scoring system that distinguishes situational language from genuine emotional distress signals; a privacy-preserving score-only storage model that enables safety monitoring without surveillance; and a graduated response calibration that redirects users toward real support proportional to detected concern level. I further propose a temporal decay function that prevents unjust accumulation of concern scores over time.
This framework does not replace existing content safety systems. It extends them into the temporal dimension they currently lack. The goal is not to prevent users from expressing emotion. It is to detect when a consumer AI product is becoming a vector for harm — and to redirect, gently, toward human connection.

title: The Cart Before the Horse: Why IRR Restoration Without a Prior Compensability Finding Constitutes Double Payment

detail.title: The Cart Before the Horse: Why IRR Restoration Without a Prior Compensability Finding Constitutes Double Payment
detail.abstract: Investment treaty tribunals have used the internal rate of return (IRR) as both a benchmark of regulatory commitment and a measure of damages. This article argues that the practice contains a structural flaw. Before any IRR-restoring award can be made, a tribunal must determine whether the exogenous variable that caused the IRR to fall is compensable under the applicable framework. Failure to make that prior determination creates a substantial risk of systematic overcompensation. We call this the prior compensability requirement. Where the requirement is ignored-where a tribunal moves from the observation that the investor's IRR has fallen below the committed return directly to an award calibrated to restore it-the award necessarily compensates the investor for market risks that the regulatory framework allocated to the investor. That is double payment by definition. A mathematical framework is developed that quantifies the overpayment in monetary terms as a function of the compensable fraction of the causative shock, the differential between the IRR and the weighted average cost of capital, and the timing of the adverse event. The framework is applied to the leading awards-RREEF v. Spain, FREIF Eurowind v. Spain, EBL/Tubo Sol v. Spain, Standard Chartered Bank v. TANESCO, and PSEG v. Turkey-and shown to have direct implications for the conduct of respondents and the scope of annulment review. The 2024 EBL/Tubo Sol award is the most recent confirmation that the IRR was always a design benchmark for standard efficient installations, not a guarantee to any specific investor, and that WACC is the appropriate proxy for the reasonable return floor.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence-generated synthetic media, commonly referred to as deepfakes, presents an unprecedented governance challenge for digital societies. Despite growing regulatory attention, particularly under the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (2024), existing frameworks remain fragmented, enforcement mechanisms are poorly defined, and technical countermeasures such as watermarking are acknowledged to be insufficient in isolation. This paper argues that blockchain technology, when conceptualised as a governance infrastructure rather than merely a technical tool, offers a governance-oriented framework for addressing the deepfake verification problem. Drawing on institutional trust theory, information asymmetry theory, and decentralised governance literature, this paper develops a three-pillar conceptual framework comprising content provenance immutability, decentralised identity anchoring, and smart contractbased compliance automation, as a foundation for trustworthy AI-generated content ecosystems. The framework is positioned against current regulatory gaps in the EU AI Act and the emergent C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) standard. The paper concludes by identifying five strategic research directions and practical implementation considerations for policymakers, platform operators, standards bodies, and future researchers. This work contributes a conceptual governance architecture that advances the emerging field of blockchain-based AI accountability systems.

title: AI Exposure and Housing Markets
affiliations: University of Tulsa - Collins College of Business and Auburn University - Department of Finance

detail.title: AI Exposure and Housing Markets
detail.abstract: Generative AI arrived just as the pandemic had pushed housing demand away from expensive, supply constrained metros. We ask whether the period after ChatGPT extended that dispersion or reversed it. Using a quarterly panel of 211 U.S. metros from 2017Q1 to 2025Q4, we relate Zillow and FHFA house price growth to AI Geography Exposure weighted by 2019 population, with the 2020 remote work break timed separately. AI exposed metros grow faster after 2023: a one standard deviation increase in AIGE is associated with 3.6% higher cumulative ZHVI growth, about $9,400 at the sample median 2023 home value. The premium also appears in FHFA prices and rents, concentrates in supply inelastic metros, and is reproduced by a predetermined LLM task suitability index. A pandemic WFH placebo has the opposite sign. IRS migration data show reduced outmigration from exposed metros, and Revelio LinkedIn data show rising AI hiring there. The early generative AI period appears to have reinforced the residential value of dense, supply constrained high skill labor markets, reversing the spatial direction of the pandemic.

title: Trade War and Persistent Imbalance: Evidence from the US-China Trade Balance after 2018
affiliations: and South China University of Technology

detail.title: Trade War and Persistent Imbalance: Evidence from the US-China Trade Balance after 2018
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the 2018 US-China trade war has fundamentally altered the persistence of bilateral trade imbalances or primarily affected short-run dynamics. Using monthly data from January 2010 to July 2025, we analyze the post-2018 evolution of trade balances and their dynamic responses to policy shocks. To capture the interaction of macroeconomic forces under structural change, we employ a Dynamic Factor Model alongside benchmark models including an Unobserved Components Model, SARIMA, VAR, and Bayesian VAR. The results show that the US-China trade imbalance remains highly persistent after the trade war, with China maintaining a stable surplus and the US continuing to experience a sustained deficit. The adjustment process is asymmetric, with larger changes occurring on the US side. Although trade tensions generate short-run fluctuations, they do not fundamentally reverse the underlying imbalance. From a policy perspective, these findings suggest that tariffbased measures alone are unlikely to achieve sustained rebalancing of bilateral trade and that deeper structural factors continue to shape long-run trade dynamics.

title: The Legal Implications of the May 13, 2026, Statement on the Restructuring of Venezuelan Debt

detail.title: The Legal Implications of the May 13, 2026, Statement on the Restructuring of Venezuelan Debt
detail.abstract: This analysis examines the legal implications of the May 13, 2026, announcement of the restructuring of Venezuela's external debt. There are three central conclusions: (i) the announcement covers all external public debt owed to private creditors, including non-financial debt arising from contractual awards and claims; (ii) under General License 58, the Government may undertake only preparatory actions, or "step zero," without authorization to negotiate directly with creditors; and (iii) these preliminary actions are informed by the general principles of administrative law, including transparency, and will be reinforced by the institutional anchorage of the International Monetary Fund.

title: French Fiscal Preferences: Results from a Representative Survey
affiliations: CNRS

detail.title: French Fiscal Preferences: Results from a Representative Survey
detail.abstract: What measures are the French willing to accept to reduce the public deficit? I analyze the results of a survey conducted in 2026 on a representative sample of 1,000 French citizens. For 30 fiscal consolidation measures, respondents indicate whether each appears desirable, appropriate, tolerable or unacceptable. The French prefer measures to rationalize public spending, taxes on the wealthy, and the elimination of welfare benefits for foreigners; they reject raising the retirement age and tax hikes affecting all households (VAT, CSG). Moreover, a majority wishes to improve public services, raise the minimum wage, or see tougher law enforcement. The tripartite division of parties between the left, centre-right/right, and far right emerges naturally from programmatic preferences. The left is distinguished primarily on the question of foreigners, the centre-right/right on pensions. Building a majority will be difficult: while most French citizens wish to control public debt, at most 34% would accept all the measures of a programme achieving the 90 billion savings required to meet that goal. The largest majority-backed package of measures would generate savings of 70 billion euros through higher taxes on the wealthiest, a freeze on public spending, and sector-specific environmental taxes. A group of deficit hawks who support any kind of fiscal consolidation measures could determine the outcome of the next election by ensuring the victory of the candidate with the most credible budget plan. Most French citizens do not fully identify with any party. Dissatisfaction with all political parties manifests in a dispersion of individual preferences, far more varied within the voters of any given party than between the average preferences of voters of different parties.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how uniform institutional grants are translated into university expenditure under unequal financial capacity. Using a 2017-2024 panel of 149 private Korean universities, it analyses Korea's University Innovation Support Program by interacting grant intensity with a pre-treatment Financial Vulnerability Index based on tuition dependence, compensation rigidity, enrolment pressure and per-student revenue capacity. The estimates provide pattern-level evidence that grant exposure is associated with different expenditure pathways across the financial distribution. Relatively healthier institutions appear more able to absorb grant exposure through adjustable administrative channels, while financially vulnerable institutions show patterns consistent with compensation-and-administration adjustment and more tentative preservation of student-facing expenditure. The paper argues that financial vulnerability should be treated as an implementation condition, and that uniform grant monitoring should be complemented by pre-disbursement financial diagnostics and differentiated stewardship.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how characteristic-based factors that account for higherorder moments developed in the equity asset class can be applied to construct optimized portfolios in cryptocurrency markets. Using a fourth-order Taylor expansion of expected utility, the analysis extends traditional mean-variance methods to capture the strongly non-Gaussian features of digital asset returns. Empirical results show that characteristics such as size, momentum, and tokenomics systematically load higher-order risks and help explain cross-sectional variation in crypto returns. Incorporating these moment exposures into the optimization process yields substantial improvements in risk-adjusted performance and portfolio stability, particularly in environments marked by asymmetry, fat tails, and liquidity frictions. Overall, the findings demonstrate that higher-moment portfolio construction transfers robustly from equities to crypto assets and provides a tractable framework for modeling their unique distributional properties.

title: The Permanent Liability Gap in AI Biometric Governance: Introducing the Biometric Irreversibility Premium — The First Financially Quantified Board-Level Measure of Compounding Permanent Liability from Biometric AI Governance Failure

detail.title: The Permanent Liability Gap in AI Biometric Governance: Introducing the Biometric Irreversibility Premium — The First Financially Quantified Board-Level Measure of Compounding Permanent Liability from Biometric AI Governance Failure
detail.abstract:
Biometric data is unique in one critical and irreversible respect: it cannot be changed. A stolen password can be reset. A compromised credit card can be cancelled. A breached biometric record — a fingerprint, a facial geometry map, a voice signature, an iris pattern — cannot be reissued, recalled, or made safe. The person whose biometric data has been compromised carries that vulnerability permanently. This single fact transforms biometric data governance from a regulatory compliance question into a compounding permanent financial liability — and it is a fact that no existing governance framework, actuarial model, or insurance product has ever financially quantified at board level. Until now.
This paper introduces PAIBG — the Picken AI Identity and Biometric Governance Assessment — and its central novel contribution: the Biometric Irreversibility Premium (BIP). The BIP is the first financially quantified, board-level measure of the compounding permanent liability created by biometric AI governance failure. It is not a qualitative risk rating. It is not a technical detection score. It is a pound figure, calculated at a stated confidence interval, that captures what every other governance framework misses: the fact that biometric breach liability does not have a finite claim window — it has a lifetime. The BIP multiplies the standard PAVR regulatory exposure calculation by the Biometric Irreversibility Multiplier, a proprietary coefficient calibrated against published ICO enforcement data showing biometric fine multiples of 2.3x to 4.1x equivalent nonbiometric enforcement actions, published court award data, and actuarial life table modelling of the permanent identity fraud cascade enabled by compromised biometric templates.
PAIBG makes three novel contributions. The BIP is the primary contribution — the first actuarial instrument for permanently compounding biometric liability that insurers, boards, and regulators have not previously had. The Biometric Governance Score (BGS) is the second — a 0-100 boardlevel governance score with full regulatory band interpretation across UK GDPR Article 9, EU AI Act, Equality Act 2010, and the ICO's named 2025-2026 enforcement priorities. The Lawful Basis Assessment (LBA) is the third — a six-stage pass/fail evidentiary framework that maps directly to the ICO's enforcement criteria and produces a signed compliance verdict for each biometric system the organisation operates.
Applied to a synthetic composite UK multi-venue operator deploying five biometric AI systems simultaneously, PAIBG identifies £287,600 in quantified governance exposure — including £33,600 in BIP that is invisible to every standard governance and insurance framework. The EU AI Act prohibition on real-time biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces takes effect August 2026. The ICO named biometric enforcement as its primary regulatory priority for 2025- 2026. The governance window is closing from both directions. PAIBG provides the board-level framework to close it proactively.

title: Ownership Structure and Performance; Does Privatization matter in Tunisia?

detail.title: Ownership Structure and Performance; Does Privatization matter in Tunisia?
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between ownership structure and firm performance in Tunisian newly privatized firms during the 2000-2020 period. Using a sample of 20 firms privatized through Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) on the Tunisian Stock Exchange, the study analyzes whether changes in ownership concentration, shareholder identity, and corporate governance mechanisms affect financial and operational performance after privatization. The analysis combines univariate comparisons of pre-and post-privatization performance with multivariate estimations. The results indicate that privatization did not lead to significant improvements in profitability indicators such as return on assets, return on equity, or Tobin's Q. However, operating efficiency improved significantly, while employment and leverage declined after privatization. The findings also show important transformations in ownership structure, characterized by a gradual reduction in state ownership and increasing participation of private and foreign investors. Ownership concentration and shareholder identity appear to play a significant role in explaining firm performance. In particular, moderate ownership concentration and foreign institutional ownership are positively associated with firm profitability and market valuation, whereas excessive concentration and persistent state ownership negatively affect performance. The results further suggest that changes in board composition and governance mechanisms contribute positively to firm outcomes. Overall, the study concludes that privatization alone is insufficient to improve firm performance unless accompanied by effective governance reforms and ownership restructuring.

title: Evading Capital Controls via Cryptocurrencies: Evidence from China
affiliations: Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College - The City University of New York, Deakin University - Department of Finance (Property and Real Estate) and University of Technology Sydney (UTS)

detail.title: Evading Capital Controls via Cryptocurrencies: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: To what extent are cryptocurrencies used to evade cross-border capital controls? We develop a new method that exploits blockchain data to identify such activities. We find that capital flight out of China is economically meaningful, accounting for over one-quarter of Chinese Bitcoin exchange volume. Capital flight increases with economic policy uncertainty and results in a Bitcoin price premium when traded against the Chinese Yuan, ruling out alternative explanations such as arbitrage. Individuals engaging in capital flight are less likely to use Bitcoin to trade illegal goods or services, suggesting that capital flight has different motivations to other criminal activities.

detail.abstract: Carbonaceous shale within construction aggregate limestone mines is highly susceptible to oxalic acid-induced deterioration, which seriously threatens the stability of engineering slopes. To clarify the acid-rock deterioration mechanism, laboratory tests, reaction kinetic analysis and multi-scale microstructure characterization were comprehensively integrated. The results show that shear strength degradation presents an obvious two-stage characteristic controlled by a critical concentration of 0.011 mol/L. This threshold divides the deterioration into slow and rapid regimes, governed by the dissolution of calcite and illite. A reliable multi-scale correlation framework is established to provide quantitative tool for evaluating acid-induced damage of carbonaceous shale in limestone mine slopes.

title: The Imports of Processed Fruit Products from Ukraine to the EU Member States After Trade Liberalization in 2022
affiliations: Poznań University of Life Sciences

detail.title: The Imports of Processed Fruit Products from Ukraine to the EU Member States After Trade Liberalization in 2022
detail.abstract: The aim of the study was to analyze how the decision to establish free trade between Ukraine and the European Union after the Russian invasion of Ukraine influenced the volume of imports of selected fruit products to the EU Member States, especially to Poland. Material and Methods: The Eurostat (Comext) database was used as a source of data showing the monthly volume (kg) of imports of fruit products (according to the CN code) from Ukraine to individual EU Member States between June 2017 and May 2024. The imports of the following fruit products were analyzed: apple juice concentrate, frozen: cherries, strawberries, raspberries, and blackcurrants. The study was based on the descriptive method and statistical methods: arithmetic mean and single-base index. Results: The liberalisation of trade with Ukraine caused an increase in the imports of most the aforementioned fruit products to the EU. The volume of imports of apple juice concentrate increased nine times, frozen blackcurrants-over seven times, frozen raspberries-three times, frozen strawberries by only 3%, whereas the volume of imports of frozen sour cherries decreased by more than a half. After the trade liberalization, processed fruit products were also imported from Ukraine by those countries which did not import them in the reference period. Poland was the largest importer of each of those processed fruit products from Ukraine. After the trade liberalization, the highest increase in the imports of apple juice concentrate, frozen raspberries, and frozen blackcurrants was observed in Poland. Conclusions: Fruit production and processing in Poland is well-developed. Further liberalization of trade with Ukraine may cause problems for fruit producers in Poland. They may experience difficulties in selling these products for processing or the sales prices may not be satisfactory.

title: Greasing or Sanding the Wheels? Political Corruption and Venture Capital Investment Decisions
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London, Dublin City University and University of Sheffield

detail.title: Greasing or Sanding the Wheels? Political Corruption and Venture Capital Investment Decisions
detail.abstract: This paper examines how political corruption affects venture capital investment decisions in the United States from 1985 to 2019. Using state level corruption convictions to measure the local corrupt environment of portfolio companies, we find that corruption reduces VC investment amounts and syndication, while increasing staged financing. These effects are economically meaningful and remain robust to various robustness tests, including instrumental variable estimation, falsification tests, and judicial district fixed effects analysis. Path analyses show that corruption discourages VC investment partly through lower syndication and higher litigation risk, with syndication playing the larger role. We also find that the adverse effects are stronger in government dependent and high technology sectors, but weaker for older firms. Corruption also reduces the likelihood of successful exits and IPO exits. Overall, the evidence supports the sand the wheel view of corruption in entrepreneurial finance.

title: Multi-field Coupled Optimization of an Air-Purifying BIPVT System with Thermal–UV Synergistic Disinfection: A CFD–Bayesian Optimization Approach

detail.title: Multi-field Coupled Optimization of an Air-Purifying BIPVT System with Thermal–UV Synergistic Disinfection: A CFD–Bayesian Optimization Approach
detail.abstract: The use of renewable energy to reduce building energy consumption has become a major trend, while indoor bioaerosol control has received increasing attention in the post-pandemic era. Air-purifying building-integrated photovoltaic/thermal (BIPVT) systems can provide power generation, space heating, and air purification without additional energy input, offering a pathway to integrate building energy efficiency with indoor health. In this study, a thermal–UV synergistic inactivation mechanism is introduced to enhance the bioaerosol control capability of such systems. However, the highly non-uniform temperature, UV radiation, and flow fields, together with multi-dimensional structural parameters, make the coordinated optimization of power generation, heating, and air purification challenging. To address this issue, Bayesian optimization is introduced for the first time into BIPVT system optimization through a coupled CFD–Bayesian optimization framework. The results show that: 1. Bayesian optimization rapidly identified high-value regions within the first 20 iterations and increased the optimal scalarized utility to 2.068, representing a 19% improvement. 2. Under equal weighting of heat gain, power generation, and air purification, high-value designs were mainly associated with moderate PV coverage and upper-channel UV lamp placement. 3. Compared with random and uniform sampling, Bayesian optimization achieved 5.1% and 15.6% higher optimal scalarized utilities under comparable sample sizes. 4. Parametric analysis further confirmed its stability and effectiveness under different UV wavelengths, channel depths, and lamp numbers, while increasing UV lamps showed limited marginal benefits beyond two lamps. The results provide insights for controlling indoor airborne disease and offer a new approach for optimizing BIPVT systems.

detail.abstract: Two-thirds of strategic value is lost between formulation and outcome, and that ratio has held for six decades despite every management innovation aimed at closing it (Mankins and Steele 2005; Arora 2026, SSRN 6488558). The dominant explanations have been behavioural and cultural: misaligned incentives, weak accountability, change-resistance, leadership churn. These accounts identify real failure modes but do not explain the ratio's persistence. This paper offers a complementary, structural reading. Strategy execution depends on a seven-stage value chain: scan, diagnose, formulate, recommend, activate, monitor, adapt. Each stage requires specific infrastructure to close at fidelity, and until 2023 no era had simultaneous access to the conditions the chain requires. The Advisory Era (1960s to 2010) was native to the upstream stages but exited at the recommendation handoff. The Platform Era (2010 to 2022) extended infrastructure into activation and monitoring but could not natively complete adaptation. The Execution Intelligence Era, opening in 2023, is the first to assemble all six structural conditions under which the loop can close end to end: foundation-model reasoning, agentic execution standards, multi-agent orchestration, real-time data at software-as-a-service economics, defined data sovereignty regulation, and human-in-the-loop architecture. Drawing on a research universe of approximately one hundred and ten organisations, the paper argues that the persistent gap is not a behavioural defect awaiting better discipline but a structural condition now addressable at its root. The persistent gap is not a verdict on prior eras; it is the visible signature of an architectural layer that has only now become buildable.

detail.abstract:
Background: Approximately 92 million Americans reside in primary care Health Professional Shortage Areas, and preventable hospitalizations generate substantial avoidable inpatient costs. Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) serve as the federal safety-net response, yet their community health worker (CHW) integration models remain reactive, heterogeneous, and underfunded.

Objectives: This policy analysis examines Brazil's Estrategia Saude da Familia (ESF) and its CHW component, the Agente Comunitario de Saude (ACS), as an evidence-based operational model with adaptation potential for U.S. FQHCs. It identifies structural analogues between the two systems, discusses the financial logic of territory-based CHW deployment, and proposes a three-component adaptation framework.

Findings: Peer-reviewed evidence consistently links ESF expansion to reductions in hospitalizations for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions (Macinko et al., 2010; Bastos et al., 2017). The most rigorously evaluated U.S. CHW program documents a Medicaid return of USD 2.47 per dollar invested (Kangovi et al., 2020). Illustrative scenario projections for FQHC territory-based deployment are calibrated against the CDC-funded systematic review of U.S. CHW programs (Rashid et al., The Lancet Regional Health Americas, 2026), which reports a national median ROI of USD 2.12 (IQR 1.64-4.03). The structural parallel between ESF teams and U.S. FQHC care teams appears closer than commonly recognized in the implementation science literature; the operational difference most amenable to adaptation is deployment logic rather than organizational design.

Conclusions: FQHCs in Texas and Florida, serving large Hispanic and immigrant populations in documented shortage areas, represent strategically plausible early implementation contexts. The author proposes a pilot design and invites collaboration from U.S.-based health organizations.

detail.abstract: Telemedicine visits, in the form of synchronous virtual interactions between patients and providers, have witnessed a significant surge during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet, little is known about the operational effects of using telemedicine. In this study, we examine the causal relationship between the form of psychotherapy treatments (virtual or in-person) and the service time of these treatments. Using visit-level patient data for psychotherapy visits in the United States (U.S.), we employ an instrumental-variable approach to estimate the causal impact of telemedicine use on monthly service time. We find that telemedicine use significantly increases monthly service time, driven by both higher visit frequency and longer per-visit service time. These effects may reflect challenges and limitations in the use of digital technologies during telemedicine visits. Heterogeneity analyses further show that retirees experience larger increases in service time than non-retirees, and treatment effects rise with patient age. These patterns could be attributed to a decline in technological literacy among older retirees. These results show that serving elderly patients, especially retirees, with telemedicine can increase the burden on healthcare providers. Our study contributes to a better understanding of how telemedicine affects the efficiency of mental health care delivery.
